title: Patrick Brammall: ‘If I find something humiliating, it’s going in the show’
author: Annabel Nugent
content:
Patrick Brammall is “blandly handsome and on the comfy side of fit”, or so said The New York Times in a 2018 article about the Australian actor. “I didn’t have a publicist back then or anything, so I thought, you know, this is amazing! Then I read that bit, and I’m like, ‘Mate, you didn’t need to write this. What are you doing?’” he laughs. It’s now eight years later, and Brammall is fresh off his role playing Anne Hathaway’s love interest in The Devil Wears Prada 2. Suffice it to say, there are no hard feelings.
In fact, “blandly handsome” was his Twitter bio for years. At 50, Brammall is used to mining his life for laughs. He knows everything, even the most cutting backhanded compliment, makes for great material. It’s why he brings that quote up today, and it’s certainly one of many reasons why his breakout hit Colin from Accounts – a charming, ribald comedy inspired, in part, by his relationship with his wife, co-star and co-creator Harriet Dyer – is so brilliant. “If Harry and I find something funny, it doesn’t matter how embarrassing it is for us; it’s going in the show,” says Brammall, recalling an early scene in which he falls out of a bathtub fully nude after accidentally sending a dick pic. “It’s humiliating. But we have to do it.”
Due to air its third and final season in the UK this month, Colin began back in 2022 with a flash, literally. Gordon (Brammall) is driving through Sydney when he locks eyes with Ashley (Dyer) who, crossing the street, flashes him a smile and a breast. Gordon is so distracted by the sexy surprise that he hits a dog – a calamity that brings these two strangers together in hilarious and oddly affecting ways. That Gordon is 12 years older than Ashley is a comic gift on telly and in real life, such as when a fan mistook Brammall for Dyer’s dad.
![Real-life couple Harriet Dyer and Patrick Brammall in romcom ‘Colin from Accounts’](https://static.the-independent.com/2023/12/04/12/423383.jpg)
His latest project sees him pulling from his life in less joyful ways. Out next week on Apple TV, Last Seen casts Brammall in a very different light. He plays Ian Ridley, a grizzled ex-police officer struggling to cope after the abduction of his three-year-old daughter, 11 years earlier. When Ian, now working as an emergency phone operator, receives a call from a girl he believes to be his missing child, he sets out on a mission to uncover the truth.
No doubt, Brammall says, being a father fed into his performance. He and Dyer have two adopted daughters, Joni and Mabel. “My eldest was three at the time we were filming, and I think that gave me a bit of a shortcut into the character that I wouldn’t have access to if I wasn’t a dad,” he says. It also helped in a roundabout way that Brammall left home to start shooting the series just 12 days after the birth of their second child. “Crazy,” he grimaces. “I was fully abandoning my family to go and film this.” Dyer and the kids followed to Melbourne, where Last Seen was being shot, as soon as Mabel’s passport came through so they could be together as a family. “But still, it’s not what you imagine you should be doing as a father, so I let the feelings of being an absent dad help inform my choices as Ian, for sure.”
Brammall is completely convincing as a gruff, unshaven alcoholic. All repressed emotion and violent desperation, Ian is very much not Gordon. But Last Seen is not as much of a switch-up as it initially seems; Brammall is a classically trained actor who made his name back home with Glitch, a paranormal two-season tale that won Australia’s top drama-series awards. Taking on a dramatic role like this wasn’t as daunting a prospect then as leading an Apple TV show in general. “A lot of people are going to see it so I didn’t want it to suck,” he says simply, considering this for a moment before adding, “but that’s every job really.”
![Patrick Brammall and Anne Hathaway in the long-awaited sequel ‘The Devil Wears Prada 2’](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/05/05/16/13/10-PER-USE-PLEASE-DO-NOT-REUSE-WITHOUT-PERMISSION-GettyImages-2228722642.jpeg)
Perhaps nowhere more than his last gig playing the boyfriend of Andy Sachs in one of the year’s, if not the decade’s, most anticipated sequels: The Devil Wears Prada 2. As the lovely Peter, an Australian real-estate contractor living in New York City, Brammall is an antidote to Nate's (Adrian Grenier) whiny dismissiveness in the 2006 original. He’s a nice guy. Too nice, some fans thought. “The most criminally tedious heterosexual male to ever appear in a mainstream movie,” read a piece published in this newspaper (sorry, Patrick), amid several others like it. Brammall is understanding of the criticism. “People are so connected to the character of Andy, and she’s been present with them for decades, so I think they have very strong feelings about what she should and shouldn’t do,” he says.
The role was also trimmed down some because, well, that’s showbiz baby. A consummate professional, Brammall is understanding of this too. “You’ve got so many characters to service, and you’ve got such a huge audience to service,” he says. “In the end, I understand the function of that character. He was a supportive guy. He was there. There was a bit of a skirmish between them [...] but not really, and then it’s a nice soft place to land at the end. I totally get it, and I didn’t take it personally.” The movie’s director, David Frankel, got in touch to let him know his scenes had been condensed before the premiere – something that Brammall makes sure to do himself when he’s the one wielding the scissors as a showrunner on Colin.
Regardless of any criticism, Peter was a plum role, a part so coveted in Hollywood that Brammall didn’t think he stood a chance – which is why he flat-out declined the invitation to audition. He was still shooting Last Seen at the time, and the family was getting ready to relocate to Montreal, where Dyer was due to start filming a workplace comedy for US television, called DMV. “So even if I got the role, I would have had to do it while I was meant to be being dad. It was inconvenient for everyone, and so I said, thank you, but no,” he says. “Also, underneath all of that, I thought, I’m not going to get it anyway, so it’s a waste of time. One week later, I got a text from the director offering it to me. No audition.”
![Breaking bad: Patrick Brammall plays a troubled ex-police officer in ‘Last Seen’](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/09/03/10/28/Last_Seen_Photo_010401.jpeg)
A little coyness goes a long way, I suggest. “It wasn’t a move on my part, but it turned out pretty well for me,” he says. “Once they offered it, I couldn’t say no, and so we had to adjust as a family. Harry was like, ‘Oh, what a nightmare! But yes, of course, you have to do that.’” He repaid the favour at the film’s star-studded premiere where he accidentally agreed with an interviewer who called Hathaway the most beautiful woman in the world. Watching from home, Dyer shared a very funny video capturing her reaction to marital betrayal caught on live television. “I’d like to take this opportunity to rescind my comment,” laughs Brammall. “Anne is very lovely, but no one’s more beautiful than Harriet Dyer… I’m never going to get over that! But hey, I was on a red carpet talking to a man in a purple trench coat. The red carpet’s a crazy place.”
With a mega blockbuster under his belt and now an Apple TV show, Brammall seems to be on his way to making good on an early comparison that The New York Times (yes, in that same article) made to American superstars Chris Pratt and Ryan Reynolds. “I don’t think I’m living in the same size houses as those guys!” says Brammall, laughing. “Fortunately, I am not in the business of making comparisons of myself to anyone, so I do not have an opinion about that.”
When you’ve got two parents whose careers are on the rise, something’s gotta give, and with their second daughter now aged one, the idea of doing another season of Colin felt impossible to Brammall and Dyer both. “We’ve been making the show for as long as our eldest daughter has been alive and so she’s always had to share us with the show, and now we’ve got the younger one… there’s just too much to do,” he says. “And it requires Harry and I both, and so that’s not ideal.” As such, this third outing will be Colin’s last.
![Dynamic duo: Patrick Brammall and Harriet Dyer pictured at the 2025 Baftas](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/09/04/8/01/GettyImages-2214519428.jpg)
It was as much a creative decision as it was a practical one, notes Brammall. “The story we’ve been telling is about two people who meet in this chaotic way and whether they choose to embrace that chaos or not, which is what we find out at the end of the third season,” he says. “If we kept going, of course it’d be fun, but it would be a different show. It’s not a show we’d ever make.”
Would he and Dyer ever be tempted to cash in and let someone, in the UK or America perhaps, do a remake? “Who knows? If they backed up a garbage truck full of money, we might have a conversation,” says Brammall. “But we’d like to leave it there. It feels special. My favourite comedies did that, and it does feel like there’s an integrity to it that I really respond to.”
The end of Colin will be a loss to the TV landscape. The singular series flourished into something emotionally resonant, sometimes even devastating, while also remaining fun and silly – the kind of show that names a veterinarian character Yvette. In that way, it is sort of like Brammall, a seasoned actor who knows that a grown man falling out of a bathtub naked will always be funny.
The first two episodes of ‘Last Seen’ are out on Apple TV on 9 September, with new episodes weekly
summary: Australian actor Patrick Brammall reflects on mining his life and embarrassing moments for comedy in his hit series Colin from Accounts, which is concluding with its third and final season. Alongside his comedic success, Brammall is starring in the dramatic Apple TV series Last Seen, drawing on his real-life experiences as a father to play a grieving ex-police officer. He also recently appeared as Anne Hathaway's love interest in The Devil Wears Prada 2, a role he initially declined before being offered it without an audition.
key_points: Patrick Brammall co-creates and stars in the comedy series Colin from Accounts with his wife and co-star Harriet Dyer, drawing inspiration from their real-life relationship.
Colin from Accounts is ending with its upcoming third and final season due to the practical and creative demands of balancing their careers and raising two young children.
Brammall stars in the Apple TV drama Last Seen as a grizzled ex-police officer searching for his abducted daughter, a role he informed with the emotional weight of being a father.
He played Peter, the supportive boyfriend of Anne Hathaway's character, in The Devil Wears Prada 2, landing the coveted role without needing to audition.

title: Richard O’Sullivan, star of 70s sitcom Man About the House, dies aged 82
author: Kevin Rawlinson
content:
Richard O’Sullivan, known for his role as Robin Tripp in the 1970s TV sitcoms Man About the House and Robin’s Nest, has died aged 82.
The actor, who was also famous for playing the title character in the TV series Dick Turpin, died peacefully with his family at his side at the Royal Variety Charity’s care home on Friday, the organisation said.
His son James O’Sullivan paid tribute to him, saying: “My dad was as funny and charming in real life as he appeared on our TV screens over the years. Always kind-spirited, good-humoured, a doting grandfather and a wonderful dad – I will miss him dearly.
“Although much of his career happened before I was born, I was fortunate enough to be able to enjoy and witness his incredible talents on the countless reruns of his shows that made him the respected and loved actor that he was.”
![O’Sullivan in the garden of Brinsworth House](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/78d75acfe34dad513b40e0061cc5c9480ad6ab73/0_192_1200_959/master/1200.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
O’Sullivan had lived at the Royal Variety Charity’s Brinsworth House in Twickenham for 23 years. His son thanked the “incredible team” there for their “love, kindness and care”. He said: “They have been truly amazing and will always hold a special place in my heart.”
O’Sullivan’s career began when he appeared in The Yellow Balloon as an eight-year-old in 1953. He later appeared in Peter Hall’s production of Love’s Labour’s Lost at the Royal Shakespeare theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1956.
He appeared in two films with Cliff Richard in the 1960s: The Young Ones in 1961 and Wonderful Life in 1964. In 1963, he starred opposite Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton in Cleopatra in the role of Pharaoh Ptolemy XIII.
![Richard O’Sullivan as Pharaoh Ptolemy XIII in Cleopatra](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/06befe2f4d64213ae60c0bd8d79df1b2dbbb7899/0_81_2079_1662/master/2079.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Man About the House ran for six series from 1973, following the trials and tribulations of a man sharing a London flat with two single women, Chrissy, played by Paula Wilcox, and Sally Thomsett as Jo.
Giles Cooper, the life president of the Royal Variety Charity, said: “Richard O’Sullivan was a master of effortless charm and impeccable comic timing, bringing pure warmth, wit, and unforgettable joy to millions of living rooms as a true giant of British television. He will be sorely missed by us all at the Royal Variety Charity.”
summary: Actor Richard O'Sullivan, best known for starring in the 1970s sitcoms Man About the House and Robin's Nest, has died at the age of 82. He passed away peacefully on Friday with his family at his side at the Royal Variety Charity’s care home, where he had lived for 23 years. Throughout his extensive career, O'Sullivan also appeared in films such as Cleopatra and The Young Ones.
key_points: Richard O'Sullivan died at the age of 82 at the Royal Variety Charity's care home.
He was famous for his roles in the hit 1970s TV sitcoms Man About the House, Robin's Nest, and Dick Turpin.
His career began as a child actor, appearing in the 1953 film The Yellow Balloon.
He starred as Pharaoh Ptolemy XIII in the 1963 film Cleopatra alongside Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton.

title: How Oasis fans cracked the Celtic Park gigs code in chip shop video
author: Catherine Lyst
content:
![Still from a video showing two boys sitting in a chip shop with a fridge full of drinks and a number of posters](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1376/cpsprodpb/2189/live/60fe27d0-a85d-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.png)
The video on official Oasis social media accounts has a number of cryptic clues
- Published
Oasis fans have uncovered a set of cryptic clues in a promo video from the band, suggesting that they will stage gigs at Celtic Park in Glasgow next year.
The Manchester rockers released the 23-second teaser on their social media accounts, showing two boys in what appears to be a Scottish chip shop.
Internet sleuths spotted sets of numbers in posters around the chippy which they worked out to be the map co-ordinates for Celtic's Parkhead stadium.
It has fuelled speculation that the band will be playing at the venue next year- possibly as the first date of a new tour.
It follows the Gallagher brothers' hugely successful reunion tour which saw them perform at 41 sold-out stadium shows in 14 countries.
This included three dates at Murrayfield Stadium, Edinburgh, in August 2025, when they played to 200,000 fans.
![Noel and Liam Gallagher at one of the Oasis reunion gigs. They are holding their arms in the air and touching hands in the middle. Liam is holding maracas in his other hand while Noel is doing a peace sign with his fingers. Other band members are in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/914/cpsprodpb/6432/live/9b5aa340-a84e-11f1-80f8-c33181935c5a.jpg)
Oasis played at 41 sold-out stadium shows in 14 countries during their reunion tour in 2025
How did fans find the co-ordinates?
The clues hinting at a Celtic Park gig include an advert for a Â£55.84 family chippy bundle and a poster for radio station Sol FM 98 92.
The numbers spell out the 55.849892N latitude of the stadium.
There is also a sticker on the fridge saying it should be kept at -4, a poster saying the daily special is priced at Â£2.05 and a taxi number featuring the area code 638.
These numbers together are -4.205638W - Celtic Park's longitude.
![Poster saying Family chippy bundle Â£55.84 with a picture showing fish and chips](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/229/cpsprodpb/1988/live/c0189790-a83b-11f1-b3a7-d5de760fef6e.png)
The clues are believed to contain co-ordinates for Celtic Park
![Poster advertising Sol FM 98 92 that also says Realization for the Nation](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/218/cpsprodpb/79e8/live/cf16a2a0-a83b-11f1-b3a7-d5de760fef6e.png)
A radio station frequency is among the numbers that make up the co-ordinates
More clues: Robert Carlyle, Irn Bru and deep-fried Mars Bar
Other Scottish clues include the actor Robert Carlyle, who features in the video for Oasis song Little by Little which plays on a TV in the background.
The chip shop fridge is filled with Irn Bru and other AG Barr brands.
One of the boys also hands over a Mars Bar to be deep fried - a Scottish chippy delicacy.
Fans have also posted theories about other "clues" on social media.
One said the position of the two boys is similar to the positions of Noel and Liam Gallagher on the front of the Definitely Maybe album, with the fridge being in a similar position to the window.

You may want to read Metaâs Instagram cookie policy, external and privacy policy, external before accepting. To view this content choose âaccept and continueâ.
An announcement has been rumoured to coincide with the release of Oasis: Don't Look Back in Anger, a documentary covering the band's reunion tour.
Recent rumours have suggested that any Celtic Park concerts could take place immediately after the Scottish football season ends in late May with Knebworth also believed to be on the cards.
The Gallagher brothers' affection for Celtic is well documented, stemming from their family's Irish roots.
The Oasis classic Roll With It has become an unofficial Celtic anthem, having first been adopted by supporters around the 1997 League Cup final.
And Noel famously attended the Old Firm game in 2000 when Celtic beat Rangers 6-2.
![Part of fridge containing drinks which says Keep fridge at -4. There is also a poster saying Daily Special We batter anything Â£2.05](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/273/cpsprodpb/6b9b/live/dbca6f90-a83b-11f1-b3a7-d5de760fef6e.png)
The clues are scattered around the chip shop featured in the video
![Part of a see-through heated counter with pies inside. There is a sign for a taxi with the number 638. There is also part of a fridge showing containing cans of drink.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/348/cpsprodpb/441c/live/70435b90-a83d-11f1-b3a7-d5de760fef6e.png)
The clues have fuelled speculation that the band will be playing at Celtic Park, possibly as part of a new tour
Celtic Park has not hosted any concerts for a number of years with the last being Wet, Wet Wet in 1997.
Other noteable gigs there have been Rod Stewart, Status Quo and Joe Cocker in 1991, Bryan Adams and Prince in 1992, U2 and Utah Saints in 1993.
Rod Stewart performed there again in 2014 during the Opening Ceremony for the Commonwealth Games.
Glasgow's Hampden Park has become the city's main concert stadium over the past three decades.
summary: Oasis fans have uncovered cryptic clues in a promotional video that suggest the band will stage concerts at Celtic Park in Glasgow next year. Internet sleuths identified sets of numbers hidden on posters and signs in a Scottish chip shop featured in the teaser, which translate to the exact map coordinates of the stadium. The band has a history with Celtic, and the potential gigs would follow their successful 2025 reunion tour.
key_points: Fans spotted numbers in the Oasis promo video that spell out the latitude and longitude coordinates for Celtic Park.
The clues included a £55.84 family chippy bundle, a Sol FM 98.92 radio poster, a -4 fridge temperature, a £2.05 daily special, and a taxi number with the code 638.
The video also featured Scottish elements such as actor Robert Carlyle, Irn Bru, and a deep-fried Mars Bar.
The Gallagher brothers have well-documented ties to Celtic, with their song Roll With It serving as an unofficial club anthem.
Celtic Park has not hosted standard music concerts for many years, with Hampden Park serving as Glasgow's main concert venue instead.

title: 6 Emmerdale spoilers for tonight as Vinny confesses everything
author: Daniel Kilkelly
content:
Emmerdale spoilers follow from Friday's episode (4 September), which is available to watch now on ITVX and YouTube but hasn't aired on ITV1 yet.
In tonight's Emmerdale, Vinny reaches breaking point and confesses his guilt over the crash – but is he trusting the wrong person?
Meanwhile, DS Ramsden ruins an important occasion for Charity, Sadie snoops around behind Nicola's back, and Kim puts pressure on Joe to sort himself out.
Read on for six big moments from Friday's episode…
1. Vinny breaks down
Vinny's guilt over the crash overwhelms him and when Gabby finds him in a bad way, she realises that she's been right with her theory about the crash all along.
Is Gabby willing to keep her ex's devastating secret, especially with the consequences so close to home?
2. Kev urges Vinny to be honest
Vinny's worries intensify when he fears that Kev overheard his conversation with Gabby. Sensing that something is wrong, Kev encourages Vinny to open up and promises a non-judgemental response to anything that he wants to share.
Cautiously believing he can trust Kev, Vinny tells him the truth about the crash but is mortified when the ex-con reacts angrily. Has Vinny made a big mistake by letting his guard down around Lewis's unpredictable father?
3. DS Ramsden strikes again
On the day of Dr Todd's funeral, Charity tries to take her mind off the evil abuser by gathering her family together for a meal.
DS Ramsden gatecrashes the occasion and summons Charity to the police station to review her original statement about Dr Todd's death, which no longer matches the evidence…
4. Sarah breaks her silence
Fearing for Charity's future, Sarah decides that it's time to tell Mack who really killed Dr Todd.
Serena is alarmed that the pact of silence she'd struck with Charity and Sarah is already crumbling. Could she be implicated in the fallout?
5. Sadie asks to be involved in Jimmy's funeral
Sadie reaches out to Nicola by offering to support her through her grief. She also asks to play a part in planning for Jimmy's funeral and is surprised when her rival agrees.
Later, Sadie seizes an opportunity to snoop around Nicola's home, but what is she looking for?
6. Kim gets tough with Joe
Kim is starting to lose patience with Joe's response to Dawn's death, especially as he has a newborn son who needs him.
Amid fears that Joe could put his child up for adoption, Kim is adamant that she won't let that happen. But is this one Tate family drama that Kim will have no control over?
More Emmerdale coverage -
Emmerdale airs on weeknights at 8pm on ITV1, and streams on ITVX.
Visit our Streaming Guide now to see at a glance where you can view ALL your favourite shows and movies.
The new edition of Legends, a 100-page all-colour celebration of Ariana Grande, is here! Buy Ariana Grande in newsagents or online.
summary: In the latest episode of Emmerdale, Vinny confesses his guilt over the crash to both Gabby and Kev, though Kev reacts angrily to the news. Meanwhile, DS Ramsden interrupts Charity's family gathering, prompting Sarah to reveal to Mack who really killed Dr Todd. Other developments include Sadie snooping around Nicola's home after offering to help with Jimmy's funeral, and Kim pressuring Joe regarding the care of his newborn son.
key_points: Vinny breaks down and confesses his guilt over the crash to Gabby and Kev.
DS Ramsden summons Charity to the police station to review her statement.
Sarah tells Mack the truth about who killed Dr Todd, alarming Serena.
Sadie offers to help with Jimmy's funeral while secretly snooping around Nicola's home.
Kim pressures Joe to step up for his newborn son amid fears he might put the child up for adoption.

title: Watch Katseye Kick Off Wildworld Tour in Dublin
author: Emily Zemler
content:
![DUBLIN, IRELAND - SEPTEMBER 01: (L-R) Daniela Avanzini, Yoonchae Jeung, Megan Skiendiel and Lara Raj of KATSEYE perform at The 3Arena Dublin on September 01, 2026 in Dublin, Ireland.  (Photo by Kieran Frost/Redferns)](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif) 
Katseye launched their global Wildworld Tour last night at Dublin’s 3Arena. The tour opener comes only days after the group cancelled their appearance at Olivia Rodrigo‘s Daisy Chain Fields Festival in Irvine, California, after member Megan Skiendiel suffered a sprained ankle.
Skiendiel was rested up for the Dublin concert, which also featured group members Daniela Avanzini, Yoonchae Jeung, and Lara Raj. Sophia Laforteza was notably missing after announcing a hiatus from Katseye in August.
The show opened with single “Hootie Frutti” and included several of the group’s hits, including “Gabriela,” “Pinky Up,” and “Gnarly.” It also featured several solo dance breaks from the singers.
Katseye released their most recent EP, Wild, on Aug. 14. It features singles “Animal” and “Pinky Up,” which arrived ahead of their Coachella debut and officially launched their first EP without Manon Bannerman, who remains on hiatus from the group. The singers have described Wild as a new era for the group. During their appearance on The Tonight Show host Jimmy Fallon asked, “How do you describe this era?” “Wild,” Avanzini said. Raj added, “I’d say maturity. Growing up.”
The Wildworld Tour will make stops in cities across North America and Europe including two nights at Los Angeles’ Crypto.com Arena. It continues with two shows in London at the O2 on Sept. 3 and 4. The North American leg kicks off on Oct. 13 in Miami.
The group teased the sold-out tour on The Tonight Show. “I feel like it will hit me once I get there because it’s our first arena tour,” Jeung said. “It’s a much bigger stage. I’m a little bit nervous. And it’s very exciting.”
summary: Katseye kicked off their global Wildworld Tour at Dublin's 3Arena, following a recent member injury and the release of their EP, Wild. The sold-out arena tour features performances of the group's hits and solo dance breaks, with upcoming stops across Europe and North America. Member Megan Skiendiel performed after recovering from a sprained ankle, while Sophia Laforteza and Manon Bannerman remained absent due to ongoing hiatuses.
key_points: Katseye launched their Wildworld Tour at the 3Arena in Dublin.
Member Megan Skiendiel performed after recovering from a sprained ankle that caused them to cancel a previous festival appearance.
Sophia Laforteza and Manon Bannerman were absent from the concert due to ongoing hiatuses.
The concert setlist included songs like "Hootie Frutti," "Gabriela," and "Pinky Up" from their latest EP, Wild.
The tour includes upcoming European and North American dates, featuring two shows in London and a North American leg starting in Miami.

title: Thieves steal 11 sheep from Clarkson’s farm
author: Ruby Cline
content:
![Jeremy Clarkson with sheep](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/03/TELEMMGLPICT000262774304_17884731366090_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqD8aGgFg7Ht8XjDF8usJqp6uC5Q2zYTqjysAlDnX0ETo.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Jeremy Clarkson with sheep](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/03/TELEMMGLPICT000262774304_17884731366090_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqD8aGgFg7Ht8XjDF8usJqp6uC5Q2zYTqjysAlDnX0ETo.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Thieves have stolen 11 sheep from Jeremy Clarkson’s farm.
Officers from Thames Valley Police are investigating the suspected late-night raid on Diddly Squat farm in Oxfordshire, which they believe took place in the last 10 days.
The TV host, 66, discovered the “awful” suspected crime when he counted his flock – to find only 16 of his 27 ‘Easycare’ sheep.
The breed, supposedly easier to care for than other sheep, do not need to be sheared and instead shed their fleeces in the summer.
Mr Clarkson estimated that the stolen flock is worth £2,000 – but the ewes could be worth up to £8,000 if they were sold for meat.
In clips of his show, Clarkson’s Farm, first seen by The Sun, the farmer said: “The police have been very good, actually.
“I said, ‘I know it’s going to sound like I’m from 1856, but I’ve had some sheep stolen’.
“She went through the name and address and then she said, ‘Oh, not your Easycares’. She’s obviously been watching the show, but it is the Easycares.”
![Jeremy Clarkson with flock of sheep](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/03/TELEMMGLPICT000315661611_17884731496820_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqxb39oh8fFGrCAqFuiQgl8t6q3K7EBk4AxZCBsIHR7d0.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
He added: “To have animals stolen, it’s really galling. They were happy here.
“They’re very good sheep. It’s upset me. You can’t ever form a bond with a sheep. Anyone who has anything stolen, it’s awful.”
Mr Clarkson said “realistically” the sheep were taken, adding: “There’s no other explanation.
“We’ve been through the woods and there are no sheep droppings in there. They’re not in the woods. They’re not on the neighbouring farm. The only option left is that they’ve been taken.”
He told The Sun: “Honestly, it just p----s me off. It’s a farm. We’re armed. Just so they know.”
The TV host said he does not think he was personally targeted.
The cost of livestock theft to British farmers is rising and totalled nearly £4.5m last year, according to the National Farmer’s Union.
The union warned that the crimes are often highly organised, with dozens of sheep stolen in single incidents.
Rural crime overall cost the South East region, including Oxfordshire, some £6.8m in 2025, according to the NFU’s annual report.
Last year, a spate of sheep thefts left farmers in Dartmoor to consider quitting their profession.
Colin Abel, a Dartmoor farmer, said he lost almost £500,000 worth of livestock after more than 400 ewes disappeared.
He said at the time: “It impacts financially and on the viability of the business. I know farmers who are thinking about whether they want to continue.”
Last year, Mr Clarkson said farmers were facing “absolute hell” as they battled rising costs on multiple fronts.
He described the “despair” faced in rural communities amid the Government’s decision to impose a 20 per cent inheritance tax rate on agricultural assets above a threshold.
summary: Thieves have stolen 11 'Easycare' sheep worth an estimated £2,000 from Jeremy Clarkson's Diddly Squat farm in Oxfordshire. Thames Valley Police are investigating the suspected late-night raid, which Clarkson discovered after finding only 16 sheep remaining from his flock of 27. The incident comes amid rising livestock theft across Britain, which cost farmers nearly £4.5 million last year.
key_points: Eleven sheep were stolen from Jeremy Clarkson's Diddly Squat farm in Oxfordshire.
The stolen 'Easycare' sheep are valued at £2,000, though they could be worth up to £8,000 if sold for meat.
Thames Valley Police are investigating the suspected late-night theft.
Livestock theft cost British farmers nearly £4.5 million last year, according to the National Farmers' Union.

title: Fun, flirty and fried to perfection: farewell to Chicken Shop Date, the YouTube show that helped kill off TV
author: Stuart Heritage
content:
When Amelia Dimoldenberg posted a video to social media this week, telling an unknown companion “we need to talk”, it felt like a monumental announcement was on the horizon. And so it came to pass. Chicken Shop Date, Dimoldenberg’s YouTube series, is coming to an end.
The press release covering the announcement came packed with superlatives. Chicken Shop Date has generated 34m hours of views over the years, and has reached 97% of all countries on the planet. What it didn’t mention is that Chicken Shop Date helped to legitimise YouTube as a platform that has taken on – and perhaps beaten – television. The very fact that the Guardian is covering the end of a YouTube video series in the first place is, in part, down to Chicken Shop Date.
Nevertheless, the writing has clearly been on the wall for some time. Dimoldenberg is moving on to bigger and better things – she hosts red carpet interviews for several major awards and is writing a romcom film, plus a YA show for the BBC – but Chicken Shop Date has also started to ossify. What began as a fun and flirty interview show, which thrived on the genuine tension that sometimes occurred between host and guest, has gradually become just another stop on the promotional cycle. It’s hard to try to flirt with someone who has quite clearly just been shoved in front of you by a publicist, as has been the case in some recent episodes (Ben Stiller, Elmo).
![Louis Theroux looks awkward in a chicken shop.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/de0bf9306ba761ddb1f59cd772a3ae33abccb236/0_0_1200_976/master/1200.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Still, it’s easy to see why the show was so popular. Dimoldenberg’s entire demeanour, simultaneously needy and passive aggressive, has made for compelling viewing over the years. In terms of sheer pop culture heft, it’s worth remembering that it was Dimoldenberg who first goaded Louis Theroux into reprising a rap he first performed in a documentary 26 years ago. It immediately went viral. Shakira danced to it on Jimmy Fallon and, despite the Chicken Shop Date redux happening four years ago, Theroux still references it approximately once every 45 seconds on his podcast.
There is also the tidal wave of interest generated by her romance (showmance? Fauxmance?) with Andrew Garfield, with whom she had shared some conspicuous chemistry on various red carpets. When he finally appeared on Chicken Shop Date in 2024, public intrigue was so high that the episode ended up getting 13m views. What’s most fascinating about this is how quickly the chemistry turned to ash as soon as the cameras started rolling. The pair looked stilted and awkward, as if they’d just realised the world expected them to be its performing monkeys. It was one of the show’s biggest moments, but also a timely reminder that not all dates are dead certs.
Other, smaller moments are just as indelible. In 2022, Matty Healy treated his appearance as an actual romantic opportunity, teasing Dimoldenberg, holding her hand and, right at the end, pestering her for a kiss for an uncomfortable length of time. In 2024, Billie Eilish played the same trick, holding Dimoldenberg’s gaze for so long that the host became visibly flustered.
Of course, purists will prefer the earlier episodes, when Dimoldenberg would use the show to deliberately weird out some much more niche British musicians. An early video, before Chicken Shop Date had established its visual identity, saw Dimoldenberg pull a variety of increasingly disgusted faces at grime MC Ghetts as he discussed the physical side of his love life.
Another, slightly later one, with Raleigh Ritchie (real name Jacob Anderson) perhaps saw the moment when the show’s potential came into clearest focus. She spent the interview chiding Ritchie for his poor posture, then seemingly provoked him into unwittingly stumbling into an immediately retracted Jimmy Savile impersonation.
It’s this essence, far more than the format or the guests, that have propelled Amelia Dimoldenberg to fame. As long as she can maintain what made her so special – the flirtiness, the awkwardness, the sense that she changed her mind about being wherever she is as soon as she got there – then she’s bound to have a long career ahead of her. If not, well … we’ll always have the chicken.
summary: Amelia Dimoldenberg has announced the end of her popular YouTube series, Chicken Shop Date, which helped legitimize digital video platforms over traditional television. While the show achieved massive global reach and cultural impact through memorable interviews with guests like Louis Theroux and Andrew Garfield, recent episodes became heavily tied to celebrity promotional cycles. Dimoldenberg is now moving on to other major projects, including writing a romantic comedy and a BBC young adult show.
key_points: Amelia Dimoldenberg's YouTube series Chicken Shop Date is coming to an end.
The show generated 34 million hours of views and reached 97% of countries globally.
Prominent episodes featured viral moments with guests such as Louis Theroux and Andrew Garfield.
The series evolved from featuring niche British musicians to becoming a standard stop on celebrity promotional tours.
Dimoldenberg is transitioning to other ventures, including writing a romcom film and a YA show for the BBC.

title: Rollicking new film Ink makes divisive media mogul Rupert Murdoch into a hero
author: Nicholas Barber
content:
Rollicking new film Ink makes divisive media mogul Rupert Murdoch into a hero
![Studio Canal Guy Pearce and Jack O'Connell stand face to face in Ink (Credit: Studio Canal)](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/images/ic/480xn/p0p7psrz.jpg.webp) Studio Canal
Danny Boyle's high-energy drama about Murdoch's early years in UK newspapers has opened at the Venice Film Festival – and its flattering portrayal of the man himself is causing debate.
Rupert Murdoch is one of the most influential media figures of the last half-century. One of the inspirations for Logan Roy in the TV series Succession, the 95-year-old mogul has reshaped the modern media world via his ownership of countless newspapers and television channels, up to and including Fox News.
Whether he has reshaped it for better or worse is a matter of debate. To some, he is a visionary businessman and a champion of the free press. Others believe that certain harmful parts of that free press can be traced back to his door.
This debate is touched upon in Ink, a rollicking new drama about how Murdoch established himself in UK media in the 1960s and '70s. Directed by Danny Boyle (Trainspotting, Slumdog Millionaire) and adapted by James Graham from his own play, Ink opened yesterday at the Venice Film Festival to enthusiastic reviews – and some questions about whether it was too soft on the tycoon at its centre.
How the film frames Murdoch
Whereas a controversial recent dramatisation of Donald Trump's early years in business, The Apprentice, portrayed its protagonist in a less than flattering light, the Murdoch played by Guy Pearce in Ink is a plucky underdog: a fearless rebel who takes on the patronising snobs of England's outdated elite. In scene after scene, aristocratic bullies sneer at him just because he is Australian – so even when they make a fair point about the damage that he is doing, they're so loathsome that it's tempting to take his side.
Some critics in Venice were sceptical. John Bleasdale in Time Out called Ink "a toothless, apolitical film" with a "bizarrely moral" Murdoch. Boyle, for his part, has said that he sympathises with the anti-establishment Murdoch of 1969. At a press conference in Venice yesterday, the director stated that, at the time, Murdoch was "a breath of fresh air in what was a very rigid British society".
The time in question is 1969. Having made his mark in Australia, Murdoch moves to London, buys an ailing British daily tabloid newspaper, The Sun, and appoints a working-class northern editor, Larry Lamb (Jack O'Connell), to reinvent it. Initially the film is staged as a high-octane heist movie, with the fast-talking, sharp-suited Lamb zipping around England, gathering a gang of misfits who have been overlooked and under-promoted by other newspapers.
His masterplan is to pinch readers from his competitors by running stories that working people actually want to read – even if that means emphasising subjects which have been sidelined by the British press elsewhere, such as sport, sex and television. And he wants to have fun while doing it, hence Ink has enough office hedonism to rival Martin Scorsese's The Wolf of Wall Street. Maybe it should have been called The Lamb of Fleet Street.
Questions about responsibility
The suggestion is that Lamb's obsession with sales figures may have led to today's populist media landscape, where nothing is off-limits. But Murdoch himself is portrayed as an almost-innocent bystander. Whenever something salacious is printed in The Sun, it's Lamb who makes the decision to run it, and Murdoch who marches into his office later and demands an explanation. Did he really have so little control over his flagship newspaper's content? In Ink, his only weakness is to be a little too squeamish, a little too hung-up on conventional decency – this despite an opening scene in which he shouts, swears and mimes sex acts in full view of the other diners in a restaurant.
More like this:
Ink is Boyle's most Trainspotting-like film since Trainspotting, what with its sex and drugs, its freeze frames and captions, its frantic energy and thumping rock songs, not to mention a stomach-turning shot of a filthy toilet. But it's also a love letter to a man who is depicted as a pioneering entrepreneur, a loyal friend and a doting father with no particular political agenda. The Murdoch dynasty might take issue with parts of the film, but they couldn't object to its portrayal of the family patriarch.
Indeed, Boyle has argued that to "monster-ise" Murdoch would absolve everyone else of their contribution to the state of today's media. In his view, everyone who consumes such media is responsible for it. As he said in Venice on Wednesday, "It was important to us that the audience feels complicit."
--
summary: Danny Boyle's high-energy drama "Ink," which premiered at the Venice Film Festival, explores Rupert Murdoch's early years entering the UK newspaper market in the late 1960s and '70s. The film depicts Murdoch as a plucky, anti-establishment underdog who bought The Sun and appointed editor Larry Lamb to reinvent it for working-class readers. However, the flattering and relatively soft portrayal of Murdoch has sparked debate among critics regarding whether the movie is too generous to the controversial media mogul.
key_points: The film "Ink" is directed by Danny Boyle, adapted by James Graham from his play, and stars Guy Pearce as Rupert Murdoch and Jack O'Connell as editor Larry Lamb.
The plot centers on Murdoch's acquisition of the ailing British tabloid The Sun in 1969 and the high-octane efforts to appeal to working-class readers with sport, sex, and television.

Critics at the Venice Film Festival debated the film's sympathetic framing of Murdoch, with some calling it apolitical while the director argued it reflects Murdoch as a breath of fresh air against rigid British elitism.
The movie places much of the responsibility for salacious content on editor Larry Lamb while portraying Murdoch as an almost-innocent bystander.

title: 'Ink': Reviews For Danny Boyle's Film About 'The Sun'
author: Andreas Wiseman
content:
!['Ink' Review -- what the critics are saying](https://deadline.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Ink_5b0c8c.jpg?w=681&h=383&crop=1) 
Danny Boyle’s tabloid drama Ink, the origin story of Rupert Murdoch’s British tabloid The Sun, has opened the Venice Film Festival.
James Graham’s script, starring Jack O’Connell, Guy Pearce (as Murdoch) and Claire Foy, is set in 1969 as the rising media tycoon acquires the daily newspaper. His partnership with editor Larry Lamb (O’Connell) turns the paper into Britain’s most influential tabloid.
The early notices have been positive so far, with the actors coming in for high praise in particular. Rotten Tomatoes is scoring the movie at 92% from 12 reviews.
Deadline’s Pete Hammond called the film “sensational” and said of the acting: “O’Connell and Pearce have never been better and really come to play here. It is a thrilling match to see them go toe to toe and watch as the power dynamics between them shift.”
Watch on Deadline
RELATED: Venice Film Festival 2026 Photos
The Times of London gave the film 4/5 stars, writing: “Flashbacks and flash forwards abound, archive headlines pulse through the dizzying frames and everywhere there’s a sense that Graham’s talky source material is being hammered into vibrant life by a director whose default setting is adrenaline overdose.”
UK outlet The Daily Telegraph also scored it 4/5, while trumpeting: “In its own down-at-heel, whisky-breathed, nicotine-fingertipped way, Ink might be Britain’s belated answer to Mad Men…”
Bilge Ebiri in Vulture was impressed, describing the drama as “electrifying” and “Danny Boyle’s best film in decades”: “While it doesn’t go for overt condemnation, the film makes it abundantly clear that the events it depicts ultimately gave birth to the solipsistic, techno-feudal morass of our present moment. It’ll infuriate many, but it might also be a masterpiece.”
Another positive review came from Screen International which hailed the “entertaining” film’s “gripping performances”, while Variety also called the movie “sizzling” and described Jack O’Connell as “superb”.
RELATED: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews From The 2026 Venice Film Festival
IndieWire was more tempered, giving the film a B score: “The lessons that British director Boyle wants to tell us by the movie’s end are groan-inducingly predictable… But Ink is bolstered by the strength of its actors, who realize characters who are never likable but are constantly fascinating.”
The Guardian gave the movie three stars, praising O’Connell’s turn, but also found faults, calling it “a lurid, violent and thumpingly unsubtle movie full of Dutch angles, cartoony shocks and gargoyle closeups.”
summary: Danny Boyle’s tabloid drama "Ink," which serves as the origin story of Rupert Murdoch's The Sun, premiered at the Venice Film Festival to generally positive reviews. Written by James Graham and starring Jack O’Connell, Guy Pearce, and Claire Foy, the film chronicles Murdoch's 1969 acquisition of the paper and his partnership with editor Larry Lamb. Critics heavily praised the lead performances and Boyle's energetic directing style, though some offered more tempered or mixed assessments of the script and stylistic choices.
key_points: "Ink" opened the Venice Film Festival and holds a 92% score on Rotten Tomatoes from early reviews.
The film stars Guy Pearce as Rupert Murdoch, Jack O’Connell as editor Larry Lamb, and Claire Foy.
Performances by O’Connell and Pearce received widespread praise from critics across multiple publications.
Reviewers compared Boyle's energetic direction favorably to past works, though a few outlets like IndieWire and The Guardian offered more mixed critiques of its subtlety and predictability.

title: Chicken Shop Date to end as host says 'time to move on'
author: Naomi de Souza
content:
![Amelia Dimoldenberg wears a blue, halterneck dress with her blonde hair down to her shoulders. Her glamorous look is is contrast with her surroundings - a mocked-up fried chicken takeaway with white, tiled walls and a black cash register on the counter.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/b41b/live/61e171b0-9ab8-11f0-b741-177e3e2c2fc7.jpg)
Amelia Dimoldenberg has been the host of Chicken Shop Date since 2014
- Published
Amelia Dimoldenberg has announced she will end Chicken Shop Date after more than a decade.
The presenter, known for her off-the-wall questions and deadpan silences, revealed the news in an Instagram post.
She has become one of the UK's best-known content creators through the web series, which features interviews with rappers, actors and celebrities framed as a "date" with the host.
While "all good dates must come to an end", Dimoldenberg told fans to expect "a few final dates" before the show officially ends.
![Amelia sits opposite Cynthia Erivo at a table in a takeaway shop. Amelia wears a glamourous, grey sparkly dress as she tucks into a chicken nugget. Cynthia, wearing a green top, looks towards the camera, her extra long, decorated nails standing out.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/7a87/live/1e825210-9a25-11f0-97f5-bd38218a3641.jpg)
Amelia has interviewed some of the biggest stars of the entertainment world, including Wicked actress Cynthia Erivo
"To me the show is my very own rom-com and I have loved creating so many stories for you to watch," she wrote.
"I am so grateful to everyone who has followed me on this journey and found some joy in these episodes.
"I never thought I'd stop Chicken Shop Date, I thought maybe it would be a part of me forever, and in some way it always will, but I feel like it's now time to move on from this adventure and on to a new one."
Dimoldenberg's most recent interviewees have included music heavyweight Paul McCartney, Swedish pop star Zara Larsson and US television host Conan O'Brien.
She previously told the BBC how Chicken Shop Date had grown out of a series of interviews with grime artists she conducted as a teenager for culture magazine The Cut.
"I started Chicken Shop Date as part of a youth club, and we made a magazine, and everything I learned there, the connections I made, the mentoring I got, set me up for the career that I have today," she said.
![Amelia wears a bejewelled pink dress with straps. She stands against a pink floral background and looks to her side, with her strawberry blonde hair sitting at shoulder length](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/819/cpsprodpb/c9ee/live/f8ee9e80-a786-11f1-b2d5-535b3b3d379f.jpg)
The star says she "never thought" she would stop Chicken Shop Date
The presenter has also been a vocal supporter of training programmes and apprenticeships to help young people into employment.
Yet success hasn't come overnight, as she told BBC Newsbeat last year.
"Some people think it's been, like, two years," she said.
"I spent so much time trying to persuade publicists, managers and talent to come on the show."
The creator said that in 2014, social media wasn't seen as the best place to promote a celebrity's latest album, film or product.
Chicken Shop Date has since gone on to rank alongside platforms like Graham Norton's chatshow or BBC Radio 1 for celebrities seeking media cut-through, she told The Guardian, external last month.
![A footer logo for BBC Newsbeat. It has the BBC logo and the word Newsbeat in white over a colorful background of violet, purple and orange shapes. At the bottom a black square reading "Listen on Sounds" is visible.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/0d6f/live/397f39f0-d40c-11ef-9fd6-0be88a764111.jpg)
summary: Amelia Dimoldenberg has announced she is ending her popular web series Chicken Shop Date after more than a decade. Known for its deadpan humor and celebrity interviews framed as dates, the show has featured guests ranging from Paul McCartney to Cynthia Erivo. Dimoldenberg stated that while it is time to move on, fans can expect a few final dates before the series officially concludes.
key_points: Amelia Dimoldenberg is ending her web series Chicken Shop Date after running it since 2014.
The announcement was made via an Instagram post where she stated it is time to move on to a new adventure.
The show features interviews with major celebrities, rappers, and actors framed as a 'date' in a fried chicken takeaway.
Dimoldenberg confirmed that fans can look forward to 'a few final dates' before the series officially ends.

title: Exclusive: Theo James reveals whether Meghan Markle will be in The Gentlemen season 3
author: Stephanie Chase; Jo Berry
content:
The Gentlemen's second season is just days away from dropping on Netflix but over the past few weeks much of the online chatter has been about the series' third season. This is due to a report saying that Meghan Markle was in talks to make her acting comeback in the Guy Ritchie show.
Deadline reported last month that Meghan was in early talks to join the show for its third season which, at the time, was yet to be greenlit.
Then, just days later, Tina Brown, the former editor-in-chief of Vanity Fair and The New Yorker, reported that Meghan had been dropped from the project due to "backlash in the UK".

Now, speaking to Digital Spy and other media ahead of season two's release, the show's lead Theo James has weighed in on the royal rumours.
“I think that is just a rumour," James said. "I don’t even know the practicalities of how one would make that happen."
Speaking about who he would like to see in the series, James added: "In terms of people that I would like to have in the series, I’d like someone psychopathic, like old school Robert Carlyle."
Last week The Gentlemen was renewed for a third season, with The Gentlemen has accelerated, the world has expanded and the consequences carry weight.
"A third season felt inevitable, and I'm looking forward to pushing the boundaries of it further."

title: Katie Price reportedly files for divorce from husband Lee Andrews
author: ITV News
content:
British media personality Katie Price is reportedly filing for a divorce from her husband Lee Andrews, after allegedly discovering his claims about being a crypto millionaire were untrue.
The Sun reported on Wednesday that the former model and businesswoman consulted a London divorce lawyer about ending her marriage.
The newspaper reported Price had split up with Andrews via WhatsApp, allegedly telling her friend she had come to her senses, adding: “Lee has lied and lied and lied. I am sick of it. It is over.”
A source told the tabloid that Andrews had promised he had £37m in a crypto wallet and would give her some of the money.
They described to The Sun how Andrews had reportedly given Price the passkey to get into his account and she “discovered it contained just $3, or £2.22”.
The source told the paper the split was “an accumulation of many things,” but the financial lie was “the final straw”.
![](https://images.ctfassets.net/pjshm78m9jt4/7MEkCd3SamUubEAqsxwB7l/87cd78be534b54025ba3d45636cdb371/katie_price.avif?fm=jpg&w=1280&h=720&q=60)
The former model has not yet commented on the alleged divorce herself.
This will be Price’s fourth divorce following marriages with singer Peter Andre, cage fighter Alex Reid and social media influencer Kieran Hayler.
In July, Price released her documentary Nothing to Hide, and she performed at Manchester Pride last weekend.

According to reports, Price ended the marriage via WhatsApp after finding only about £2.22 in his crypto wallet instead of the promised £37m. Price reportedly ended the marriage via WhatsApp message.

key_points: Kirstie Allsopp was rushed to hospital in an air ambulance after slipping on a muddy path near Welcombe Mouth beach in Devon.
Her son Oscar ran to get help before RNLI volunteers, paramedics, and Cornwall Air Ambulance crews located her.

She stated she will use a boot and crutches during her recovery period.

title: Ariana Grande ends London tour in tears before stepping back from public life
author: Shahana Yasmin
content:
Ariana Grande completed her 41-date Eternal Sunshine tour with an emotional final performance at London’s O2 Arena on Tuesday, before stepping back from public life for an extended break.
The 33-year-old singer became tearful during the sold-out show, which brought her 10-night London residency and the three-month tour to a close.
Speaking to the audience from the stage about halfway through the two-hour concert, Grande thanked fans for making the tour “one of the most beautiful, extraordinary experiences of my life”.
“I just want to express my gratitude without sobbing completely,” she told the crowd, according to Variety. “But really, thank you from the bottom of my heart, it’s been so special and I’ll cherish this experience always. I have the best fans in the entire world and I always have.”
“And I love your outfits, I love your faces, I love seeing you, I love connecting with you in this way. Thank you for all of your effort for making this so special,” she added. “All your messages and your costumes and your wardrobe and makeup is just so beautiful. I have loved every minute of this with you all and I just want to make sure I express how grateful I am. Thank you, and I love you so much.”
![Ariana Grande completed her 41-date Eternal Sunshine tour with an emotional final performance at London’s O2 Arena](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/05/20/Philanthropy-Ariana_Grande_96_16.jpg)
Grande began the tour with three shows in Oakland, California, in June and went on to perform a total of 41 shows across North America and London, with the final 10 taking place at the O2 Arena. Just like her penultimate show, she wore flat, above-the-knee boots, having announced earlier that she would need to wear “cosy footwear” on stage after suffering a “deep cut” to her foot.
The Wicked star also changed the lyrics to “thank you, next”. “Wrote some songs about Ricky/I’m tryna make him my last,” she said, referring to former boyfriend Ricky Alvarez. While the “Side to Side” singer didn’t confirm publicly that they were back, she made an Instagram post in August of the two together.
In a review of Grande’s show, The Independent’s Adam White wrote that the staging was “confined to the burnt-out husk of a house, which is first engulfed in flames, then weeds, then flowers, while police car sirens and helicopter spotlights suggest violent state surveillance”.
“The show’s ethereal closer – in which Grande, her body slack and floating, is absorbed into a great, white light in the rafters of the O2 – is beautiful yet strangely morbid. Is this a symbolic... death?” he wrote. “Whatever we’re meant to take from all of this, it undoubtedly feels like a goodbye.”
Grande’s decision to step back from the spotlight comes after months of intense public scrutiny of her appearance and health.
In a statement issued in August, the singer said she looked forward to “finishing the tour and ending it on a high note, both healthily and happily, and then taking a much-deserved break from public-facing work and appearances, which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny”.
At a show in Chicago soon after, the “we can’t be friends” singer read from a prepared note, telling her fans that the announcement wasn’t “a reactive or impulsive thing”. “It’s something that I had decided to plan,” she said.
![Grande had been due to appear in the forthcoming London revival of Stephen Sondheim’s Sunday in the Park with George opposite Wicked co-star Jonathan Bailey, who announced on Tuesday that he too was withdrawing from the production](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/09/01/16/48/GettyImages-2185976940-bfaf8eea.jpeg)
Her hiatus will take her out of the forthcoming London revival of Stephen Sondheim’s Sunday in the Park with George at the Barbican. Grande had been due to appear opposite her Wicked co-star Jonathan Bailey, who announced on Tuesday that he too was withdrawing from the production.
“Ari is one of my dearest friends, and my support for her is unwavering. Marianne is extraordinary and one of my longest collaborators and friends. After much consideration, I have decided to also step back from Sunday in the Park with George,” the 38-year-old said in a statement shared on social media.
Grande will be seen next in Focker-In-Law, the latest instalment in the Meet the Parents franchise, due to arrive in cinemas on 25 November. Directed by John Hamburg, who co-wrote the previous three films in the series, the comedy reunites Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro, with Grande playing Olivia Jones, a former FBI hostage negotiator who is dating Stiller’s character Greg Focker’s son, Henry.
For anyone struggling with the issues raised in this article, eating disorder charity Beat’s helpline is available 365 days a year on 0808 801 0677. NCFED offers information, resources and counselling for those suffering from eating disorders, as well as their support networks. Visit eating-disorders.org.uk or call 0845 838 2040
summary: Ariana Grande concluded her 41-date Eternal Sunshine tour with an emotional final performance at London’s O2 Arena before taking an extended break from public life. The hiatus follows months of intense public scrutiny regarding her appearance and health. As part of her step back from the spotlight, Grande withdrew from the upcoming London revival of Sunday in the Park with George.
key_points: Ariana Grande finished her 41-date Eternal Sunshine tour with a sold-out performance at London’s O2 Arena.
She announced plans to take a prolonged break from public-facing work following months of intense public scrutiny.
Her hiatus includes withdrawing from the upcoming London revival of Sunday in the Park with George at the Barbican.
Co-star Jonathan Bailey also announced he was stepping back from the same theatrical production.

title: From petrol pump attendant to Dylan-feted rocker and Judd Apatow muse: the delightfully unlikely life of Graham Parker
author: Alexis Petridis
content:
To say Graham Parker enjoyed a swift rise to fame is an understatement. He played his first live show with his most famous backing band, the Rumour, in October 1975, at the Newlands Tavern, a pub in Nunhead, south-east London. By the start of the following year, he had a record deal and was in the studio recording his debut album, Howlin’ Wind. The buzz around him was such that the sessions were interrupted by the arrival of a succession of stars – Thin Lizzy’s Phil Lynott among them – intrigued to hear what the fuss was about: a petrol pump attendant from Surrey who sang like Van Morrison and had written a set of smart, sharp, literate songs in between filling up cars.
The record arrived in April 1976 to vast critical excitement, a lot of it occasioned by the album’s closing track, the reggae-influenced, attitude-laden Don’t Ask Me Questions. After Howlin’ Wind came out, followed in October by Heat Treatment, things ratcheted up another notch. Parker turned up in Australia to discover the media waiting for him and a press conference arranged in the airport: they had taken the amount of music press coverage Parker was receiving to mean he was “as big as Bruce Springsteen, which was insane”. Low down on a festival bill topped by Bob Dylan, he found himself backstage collared by the headline act, eager to tell Parker how much he loved his work. There also exists a photo of Parker in Los Angeles, with, of all people, Michael Jackson, but their meeting was apparently less successful. “I said to him: ‘Michael, great to meet you, I did a version of [Jackson 5 hit] I Want You Back recently.’ And he just sort of said: ‘Ooh.’ So that,” he laughs, “was the full extent of my conversation with Michael Jackson.”
![Graham Parker in January 1976.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/419f4e9a50ef52d032de0804ca8db480306212e3/0_0_2480_3507/master/2480.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
In truth, Parker seemed an unlikely candidate for a saviour of rock. He was short and wiry, a former hippy who had taken himself off to Morocco in his teens and served time in a band called Terry Burbot’s Magic Mud: “My idea,” he sighs, “a burbot being a fish that I knew had become extinct in England because Angling Times offered £100 to anyone who could prove they’d caught one.” On returning, he went back home to Deepcut in Surrey, shorn of his “arse-length” hair, writing songs influenced not by prevalent trends (“I thought progressive rock needed to be destroyed thoroughly”), but the music he’d loved in his youth: Motown, soul, ska, “pop hits on the radio”.
On today’s video call from his home in upstate New York, ahead of a UK tour, Parker’s eyes are shielded by tinted sunglasses. Decades ago, dark glasses were his permanent look, which helped give Parker the air of a man who was almost disproportionately angry, or at least a lot angrier than his songs suggested he was. On Howlin’ Wind, he spat out the lyrics of Lady Doctor as if they were a ferocious broadside against the establishment, rather than about fancying a female GP. “Correct,” he nods. “If you went to see a band in the suburbs back then, the audience sat cross-legged, so I thought, we’ve got to do the opposite, get people up and dancing instead of sitting. So I just went out and yelled.”
The thing was, Parker didn’t seem to think his sudden rise to fame was at all unlikely. He may have looked a little incredulous in the photo of himself backstage with Dylan, but that was the exception. “Oh no, I was brimming with confidence,” he says, smiling. “I’d infused myself with this rather melodramatic idea that I was the kiddy, you know: I’m going to be the one who shows people something that can be done – attitude, great lyrics that say something, a tight band. I got an instant record deal, I was getting all this attention and none of these people who’d been slogging around the pubs for years were. I remember one of the early gigs we did, the great Ian Dury and his minder, Fred ‘Spider’ Rowe, standing in front of the stage wearing sunglasses, trying to put the mockers on me. I thought: I’m having a great effect here. This is good! I can’t help being this good, you know!” He suddenly looks a bit concerned at revealing his youthful cockiness. “I hope,” he says quietly, “you can write this up with some humour in it. I do know I was being an idiot.”
Of course, Parker never quite became the huge star everyone seemed to think he would be in 1976. Instead, he carved out a fascinating 50-year career as a critically lauded, cult singer-songwriter whose work has ranged wildly. He recorded an album of obscure Lennon and McCartney songs with Kate Pierson of the B-52s; published novels and short stories; and maintained a pretty startling level of quality control over the course of 47 albums, despite his belief that “you should press the reset button” with every new release. His most recent, 2023’s Last Chance to Learn the Twist, was a delight, a live-sounding collection of songs that range in style from soul to prewar pop.
His career has also regularly involved Parker doing the exact opposite of what one might have expected under the circumstances. In the late 70s, dissatisfied with his then record label, Mercury, he terminated their relationship by releasing Mercury Poisoning, a spectacularly withering song that, among other accusations, suggested the label “couldn’t sell kebabs to the Greeks” (“a bit literal,” he concedes today). His commercial stock rising in the 80s US, thanks to 1979’s superb Squeezing Out Sparks album, he signed a deal with Atlantic Records, whose chair Ahmet Ertegun suggested he make his next album sound “like Phil Collins”. Parker proceeded to make the deliberately rough-hewn The Mona Lisa’s Sister: a wonderful collection of songs utterly out of step with mainstream 80s rock trends, that, one can’t help but notice, has aged rather better than most mainstream 80s rock.
![Graham Parker and the Rumour performing at Reading festival in 1977.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/03099631717d7c90af55ca0e53a651ef45a5ebe3/330_295_3248_2601/master/3248.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
In 2012, he unexpectedly found himself in Hollywood at the behest of Judd Apatow, a long-term fan: a golden opportunity that might nevertheless have given another artist pause, given that Parker was required to play himself in This Is 40, one of a plethora of underperforming artists who Paul Rudd’s record label honcho character has put his faith in. “He’s signing all these losers from the 70s and 80s. He’s got Haircut 100, and Frank Black without the Pixies, and me,” Parker says, chuckling. “When Judd told me, I said: I can do this, I could destroy his record company instantly, mate. I’m in.”
after newsletter promotion
Hollywood was another entirely unexpected state of affairs. “For me, small timer, quite happy with his little career – playing grungy little solo gigs, doing records my way with no one interfering – to suddenly become this actor, pop singer thing, I didn’t see that coming. I ended up sitting in a dressing room with John Lithgow and Paul Rudd and Megan Fox, thinking, I should call a cab, I don’t belong here. But I sank into it pretty good. Being flown to Hollywood to do talks, first class, put up in these amazing hotels … I’m suddenly somebody, for five minutes. But it was a long five minutes, because the film went on and on in America, it was shown for months.”
Parker does, indeed, seem perfectly contented with his little career, grungy solo gigs and all: that’s exactly what he’s doing in the UK this month. For all his vaulting ambition in his early 20s, he is not sure that he was really cut out for fame. “The little bit of stardom I had, when everyone’s after you, everyone’s trying to grab you, that crept in and it was quite unpleasant really. Record labels start giving you too much money for music that I knew wasn’t for everybody and probably wasn’t going to burst out in platinum sales. I ended up telling my manager, tell them to pay me half what they’re offering. Which is weird, I know, but I think I did the best thing.”
![Parker performing in New Jersey in 2019.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/603883f985c672f59602e94f657fcea5abc45b12/116_186_3040_2432/master/3040.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Indeed, he is a vociferous advocate for keeping things small-scale. “I can pull a crowd, I can do it without the costs of a band, and it taught me to sing – I realised I don’t have to go out and grab the audience by the lapels, I can talk to them.” Although he has caveats. His mordantly funny 2001 song I’ll Never Play Jacksonville Again details the true story of a gig at which Parker ended up playing to “two couples, two barmen who looked like Ted Nugent, and a guy who looked a bit gormless and kept staring at one of the women’s legs until her boyfriend head-butted him. Five people in the audience and there’s a fight! How fucking often does that happen, man? I thought, this is the end.”
He says he’s been true to the song’s title and never played Jacksonville again. “But only because nobody’s offered me a gig there. If the money’s good enough and there’s two other gigs nearby, maybe I’ll do it. And I’ll do that song. It’ll be fun.”
summary: Graham Parker experienced a rapid rise to fame in the mid-1970s with his backing band, the Rumour, after transitioning from a petrol pump attendant to a critically acclaimed singer-songwriter. Despite early expectations that he would become a massive mainstream star, he instead built a diverse, 50-year cult career spanning 47 albums, literature, and unexpected acting roles like appearing in Judd Apatow's film This Is 40. Parker ultimately embraced a smaller-scale, independent approach to his music and touring, finding contentment away from major superstardom.
key_points: Graham Parker went from working as a petrol pump attendant to securing a record deal and releasing his debut album, Howlin’ Wind, in 1976.
Early in his career, he drew praise and attention from major artists like Bob Dylan and received extensive music press coverage.
Rather than achieving massive mainstream superstardom, Parker maintained a critically lauded 50-year career consisting of 47 albums and various literary projects.
He famously resisted commercial pressures from record labels, such as refusing Atlantic Records' suggestion to make his music sound like Phil Collins.
Parker unexpectedly expanded into acting, playing himself in Judd Apatow's 2012 film This Is 40.

title: Gary Glitter pleads not guilty to historical sex offence charges
author: Sam Harrison; Paul Glynn
content:
![File photo dated 28/1/2015 of Gary Glitter, wearing sunglasses, a black hat and red and white spotted scarf](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/4785/live/81ea8370-901c-11f1-b783-f784376ffc11.jpg)
Gary Glitter, whose real name is Paul Gadd, pictured in 2015
- Published
Gary Glitter, the former singer whose real name is Paul Gadd, has pleaded not guilty to eight allegations of sexual abuse against a girl when she was aged between eight and 11.
Gadd, 82, is accused of offences against the girl between 1978 and 1981, after allegedly giving her chocolate and inviting her to his home in Kensington and Chelsea, west London.
It is alleged he caused the girl to touch his genitals and "engaged in unlawful sexual intercourse" with her.
At Southwark Crown Court on Wednesday, Glitter appeared via video-link from prison to enter his pleas.
He denies four charges of indecent assault with a girl under the age of 13, two counts of sexual intercourse with a girl under the age of 13, and two counts of indecency with a child under the age of 13.
All charges relate to the same individual, and are alleged to have taken place between 12 March 1978 and 31 December 1981.
Gadd was wearing blue headwear, a blue shirt and a navy jacket, and was sitting next to a member of his legal team whilst on the call.
He spoke first to confirm his name. Then, he spoke again with his arms folded to deny the eight counts against him.
Gadd said he was "absolutely not guilty" to two of the eight charges, and repeated "not guilty" to the remaining six.
Judge Tony Baumgartner adjourned the case for a three-week trial starting on 22 November 2027.
The allegations were first reported to the Metropolitan Police on 9 January 2025 and an investigation into the circumstances was launched.
Gadd was first interviewed on 22 July last year in relation to the investigation.
The Met said in July that the alleged victim was being supported by specialist officers and had been made aware that Glitter had been charged.
The 82-year-old was one of the biggest pop stars of the 1970s with a string of number one hits.
summary: Former pop singer Gary Glitter, whose real name is Paul Gadd, has pleaded not guilty to eight historical sexual abuse charges involving a young girl between 1978 and 1981. The 82-year-old entered his pleas via video-link from prison at Southwark Crown Court. Judge Tony Baumgartner adjourned the case for a three-week trial set to begin on November 22, 2027.
key_points: Gary Glitter pleaded not guilty to eight allegations of sexual abuse against a girl aged between eight and 11.
The alleged offences took place between March 1978 and December 1981 in west London.
The charges include indecent assault, unlawful sexual intercourse, and indecency with a child under the age of 13.
A three-week trial has been scheduled to begin on 22 November 2027.
The allegations were initially reported to the Metropolitan Police on 9 January 2025.

title: First Thing: Duane Keith Davis found guilty of 1996 murder of Tupac Shakur
author: Martin Belam
content:
Good morning. A Las Vegas jury has found the former South Side Compton Crips gang leader Duane Keith Davis guilty of the murder of Tupac Shakur, bringing the case to a close nearly 30 years after the rapper was gunned down. The jury took about three hours to reach a guilty verdict in a case that relied heavily on multiple confessions from Davis himself.
The 63-year-old, who was accused of instigating the deadly shooting but not pulling the trigger himself, had spent years telling investigators and interviewers alike of his direct involvement before he was arrested in 2023.
- 
  Who was Tupac Shakur? Shakur was born in 1971 in East Harlem, New York, and rose to fame in the early 90s with lyrics that doubled as a sharp commentary on social injustice including systemic racism and police brutality. He was 25 when he died, is regarded among the greatest rappers to ever live, and continues to be celebrated around the world years after his life was cut short.
- 
  How have his family reacted to the trial? “We’ve been waiting 30 years to grieve properly,” Zayd Akinyela, Shakur’s cousin, told reporters outside the courtroom when the trial was under way. “A lot of people don’t get to grieve until they understand what happened to their loved one and how it happened.”
- 
  Why have authorities been so heavily criticised over the case? Las Vegas police faced criticism that they had bungled the investigation and failed to pursue crucial leads, including from a member of Shakur’s entourage who claimed he could identify the shooters. That witness died weeks later in a separate shooting.

The army secretary, Dan Driscoll, has handed his resignation to Donald Trump, the White House said Monday, becoming the latest high-profile figure to depart the defense department.
The resignation comes after months of turmoil at the defense department, from leak investigations and budget issues to the ousting of several senior officials including the army chief of staff, Randy George, in April. In June, the army commander of forces in Europe and Africa, Gen Christopher Donahue, unexpectedly stepped down.
- 
  What role had Driscoll been playing? An Iraq war veteran, tech investor and former adviser to JD Vance, Driscoll was tapped for the unusual role of key negotiator to try to end the war between Russia and Ukraine. A 17-year-old North Carolina girl who recorded a live stream of a shooting that killed three people at a San Diego mosque and disseminated the attackers’ white-supremacist writings has been charged with murder by aiding and abetting, a district attorney said.
The Forsyth county district attorney Jim O’Neill said the girl, whose name was not mentioned during the news conference, was arrested last week. On Monday a grand jury indicted her on three counts of murder and one count of conspiracy. Under North Carolina law, the aiding and abetting charges carry the same penalties as if the girl had committed the attack herself, O’Neill said.

We are used to the idea that our fellow humans may intentionally mislead or manipulate us, but the idea that machines can now do the same is deeply unsettling, as Snigdha Poonam’s long read explores.
