Jonathan Bailey steps away from 'Sunday in the Park with George' at the Barbican
Stephen Sondheim and James Lapine’s Pulitzer Prize–winning musical was inspired by Georges Seurat's painter A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte.
Summary
- Jonathan Bailey withdraws from Sunday in the Park with George weeks after Ariana Grande's exit
- The show comes to the Barbican in 2027
- Marianne Elliott is set to direct
![Olivia Rook](https://images.ctfassets.net/6pezt69ih962/2AnVizCwXsbKHoScEZBHKl/7b2e062e88ede030d9eea0db2bb6a632/Author_bio_pic_for_website.jpg?w=32&h=32)
Wicked and Bridgerton star Jonathan Bailey has withdrawn from the upcoming revival of Sunday in the Park with George, which is due to open at the Barbican in 2027.
Bailey revealed the news in a story posted on Instagram, which reads: "Ari is one of my dearest friends, and my support for her is unwavering. Marianne is extraordinary and one of my longest collaborators and friends. After much consideration, I have decided to also step back from Sunday in the Park with George.
“This brilliant, introspective musical has been a real passion project for me, and I feel incredibly lucky to have shared in its journey with this team. Among many things, the story explores the deep connection between George and Dot, a beautiful, devoted pairing, and I so look forward to seeing what the team, and the two actors who will now take on these roles, will create with it.
“I wish the very best to the entire company with what will no doubt be an incredible production, and I will be cheering them on as they continue this journey.”
Grande's final London show as part of her Eternal Sunshine tour takes place tonight (1 September).
Stephen Sondheim and James Lapine’s Pulitzer Prize–winning musical was inspired by Georges Seurat's painter A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte. The musical focuses on George, a fictionalised version of Seurat, as he creates his masterpiece, and his great-grandson, as he struggles with creative burnout a century later.
The show will be directed by Tony and Olivier winner Marianne Elliott, who previously collaborated with Bailey on Cock and Company. The production will also feature set design by Tom Scutt.

title: Jonathan Bailey Exits ‘Sunday in the Park With George’ After Ariana Grande Bows Out
author: K J Yossman
content:
Jonathan Bailey is the latest star to exit a West End revival of “Sunday in the Park With George” after Ariana Grande bowed out last month.
The London show was set to be an opportunity for the “Wicked” stars to reunite live on stage with Bailey playing painter George Seurat while Grande starred as Dot and Marie. They previously co-starred in the double feature franchise as Fiyero and Glinda respectively.
“After much consideration, I have decided to step back from ‘Sunday in the Park with George,’” Bailey said in a statement, in which he called “Ari” one of “my dearest friends.”
Popular on Variety
“This brilliant, introspective musical has been a real passion project for me, and I feel incredibly lucky to have shared in its journey with this team,” he continued. “Among many things, the story explores the deep connection between George and Dot, a beautiful, devoted pairing, and I so look forward to seeing what the two actors who will now take on these roles will create with it.”
“I wish the very best to the entire company. I will be cheering them on as they continue with this production,” Bailey added.
Grande revealed she was set to drop out of the Stephen Sondheim musical last month as she took “a step back from visibility” following the wrap of her “Eternal Sunshine” tour in London.
Her decision came after the release of her latest music video, for “Petal,” prompted much discourse online about her physical health.
A rep for Empire Street Productions, who are producing “Sunday in the Park with George,” confirmed the show will still go on at the Barbican Centre in London.
“Work on the production continues,” the producers said in a statement. “Casting discussions are actively under way, and the creative team is reshaping the production around a new company while preserving the ambition and artistic integrity of Stephen Sondheim and James Lapine’s musical.”
The revival is due to take place early next summer with Marianne Elliot directing and new casting will be announced “in due course.”
summary: Jonathan Bailey has exited the West End revival of "Sunday in the Park With George" following Ariana Grande's departure from the production last month. The "Wicked" co-stars were originally set to reunite on stage as George Seurat and Dot, but both have now stepped away from the musical. Producers confirmed that the show will still proceed at the Barbican Centre in London next summer, with new casting discussions currently underway.
key_points: Jonathan Bailey withdrew from the West End revival of "Sunday in the Park With George."
His exit follows Ariana Grande's departure from the production last month.
The pair previously co-starred together in the film franchise "Wicked."
Empire Street Productions confirmed the show will still go on with a new company and delayed casting announcements.

title: How the conviction of Duane Davis could help inspire efforts to find the killer of the Notorious B.I.G.
author: Christal Hayes; Anoushka Mutanda-Dougherty
content:
Watch: What it was like inside court for Tupac Shakurâs murder trial verdict
- Published
The conviction of Duane "Keffe D" Davis in Las Vegas has brought an end to one of the world's most famous unsolved murder cases.
He was found guilty of the murder of rapper Tupac Shakur, who died when the black BMW he was travelling in was sprayed with bullets in a drive-by shooting in 1996.
"This is huge. It was a tough case. It's a cold case," former prosecutor Neama Rahmani told the BBC. "We're talking about the greatest rapper of all time, an icon, and not a single arrest or prosecution for 30 years."
The conviction gives closure to Shakur's family, and has prompted questions from observers as to what it could mean for an almost identical case - the unsolved murder of Notorious B.I.G. or Biggie Smalls, also known by his legal name of Christopher Wallace.
![Duane Davis stands during a break in closing arguments in his murder trial,](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/a1c4/live/b225dba0-a5c2-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Duane Davis knew Wallace and was at the same party the night Wallace was killed
Wallace, a New Yorker, was once one of Shakur's friends, but the two became rivals and embodied the East Coast-West Coast feud that dominated 1990s hip-hop. Wallace was killed in Los Angeles a few months after Shakur and in similar circumstances - a drive-by shooting. No one has ever been charged.
"Tupac's murder and Biggie's murder are two of the great cultural touchstones of our lives," said Justin Tinsley, a journalist for ESPN's Andscape and the author of "It Was All a Dream: Biggie and the World That Made Him."
"Those two men, they were so unique, talented, and impactful, separately," Tinsley told the BBC. "But it's impossible to tell each of their stories without telling the other's."
"When you talk about these cases, they're always going to be connected because there are so many mutual figures involved with them, and ancillary figures," he said.
Theorists have long believed the two murders were linked. Wallace's name came up during Duane Davis' trial. He and Davis were at the same party the night Wallace was killed, and police interviewed Davis about it.
The investigator who conducted that interview even testified at the Tupac murder trial.
![In this black and white photograph taken in Brooklyn outside his mother's house, Wallace is in the foreground wearing a big leather jacket and a beret. He is standing next to a car and rolling a cigar while his friends stand in a group behind him. On the right you can see down what looks like a New York street](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/46de/live/f0b13940-a5eb-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Notorious B.I.G. is a hip-hop legend
The breakthrough in finally solving the Shakur case largely came down to one thing: Davis' own words.
Through documentaries with the media, his own memoir, podcasts and even a secret police interview, he acknowledged his role in Shakur's death.
Davis said he tossed a firearm in the backseat and his nephew, Orlando Anderson, used the gun to fatally shoot Shakur as they pulled up alongside his vehicle in Las Vegas on 7 September, 1996.
Anderson was shot dead in 1998, having denied killing Shakur.
During the trial, there were no eye-witnesses to place Davis as being in the car, no murder weapon presented, no video or photo evidence. His defence team went as far as to argue there wasn't even proof that he was in Las Vegas that night.
Rahmani said it was a difficult case to prosecute. He noted the rumours and speculation surrounding Davis were nothing new and had been around for decades - but the decision to charge him and go to trial was an "uphill climb" - a gutsy move - for prosecutors.
"Look, when you're a prosecutor, you're expected to win every time. They made a difficult decision to charge a case that a lot of people thought might be a loser," he explained. "And they got justice, where other people didn't even bother trying."
Davis' attorney Michael Sanft asked the jury to consider "what facts do you have?" He urged the panel, before they decided their guilty verdict, to discredit his client as a liar who told tales to sell books and make money.
"There's no proof," he argued to the jury.
The moment the guilty verdict was read in court, there was an outpouring of emotion among Shakur's family. Some cried and wiped tears with tissues. Others hugged and held hands. A family member embraced one of the prosecutors in the case.
![Friends and family members of rapper Tupac Shakur, including his sister Sekyiwa Shakur, line up to hug Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/b1dc/live/1188a690-a5c3-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Trial lawyer attorney Shaun Kent said the case really evolved with each interview and moment that Davis decided to talk about the case.
"There are no other witnesses, besides him," Kent told the BBC before the trial, noting that the "strongest witness against him, is him".
Rahmani believed Davis likely would have never faced charges if he had stayed silent.
"He really couldn't stop himself," Rahmani added. "Even when he was arrested and in custody, he was giving interviews."
Much of the Shakur trial forced the jury to place themselves back in the 1990s, at a time of intense gang violence that had infiltrated roots into hip-hop music and rivalries between East-Coast and West-Coast rappers.
It was a time of deep-rooted mistrust in policing and a street code that forbade reporting to authorities.
Even Shakur, after being hit multiple times in the drive-by shooting that would later kill him, refused to talk to authorities. "We'll take care of it," he said in an ambulance as an officer tried to question him.
The silence was echoed months later in the shooting death of Biggie Smalls.
Biggie, one of the biggest East Coast rappers, was leaving an after-party in Los Angeles for the Soul Train Music Awards, when a black Chevrolet pulled up to his vehicle at a red light and opened fire on 9 March, 1997. It was almost exactly six months after the shooting that killed Shakur, one of the biggest West Coast rappers.
![Rapper Notorious B.I.G. AKA Biggie Smalls (Christopher Wallace) receives Billboard Music Award on December 6, 1995 at The Coliseum in New York City,](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/977/cpsprodpb/095a/live/d4aded10-a5c3-11f1-8543-aba44f51f79c.jpg)
Notorious B.I.G. at an awards ceremony in 1995
Both were Grammy-nominated artists at the top of their genre, making millions and receiving constant radio play. Their fued spilled over into their lyrics, and also led to threats and physical violence.
Violence erupted on the streets of Los Angeles following both shootings, as street gangs sought to hold one another accountable for the rappers' deaths.
For years, neither murder led to arrests or convictions, just rumours and conspiracies.
"People will search for closure in any way they can get it," Tinsley said. "People are trying to make sense of it for 30 years."
Like Shakur's death, countless theories and names have surrounded the death of Biggie in Los Angeles, but the Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) have not made any arrests.
"It's really a stain on the LAPD. The fact that this could happen and not a single arrest was made and no one was prosecuted," Rahmani said, noting Biggie's killing happened on a public street in the middle of the second most populous US city.
"Prosecutors don't like to lose," Rahmani explained. "But, maybe this [Tupac's conviction] will embolden folks in Los Angeles to maybe take another look at it, a cold case that's coming up on 30 years."
Asked about the cases and whether the Tupac murder conviction could revive Biggie's death, the LAPD told the BBC that it was aware of the conviction and the investigation into Biggie's case remained active.
"The murder of Christopher Wallace remains an open, unsolved case within LAPD's Robbery-Homicide Division," Lt Elpidio Orozco said, urging anyone with any tips to call authorities.
Though Wallace's case has gone cold, the public's interest has not.
"They've been gone longer than they've been alive," Tinsley said, "But the enduring mythology around these guys and their deaths will always be a topic of conversation."
Kayla Epstein contributed to this report.
![A picture of Tupac along with the words 'Fame Under Fire: The Tupac Murder Trial', against a red and black background](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1536/cpsprodpb/9486/live/159cd370-a5bc-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.png)
summary: The conviction of Duane "Keffe D" Davis for the 1996 murder of Tupac Shakur has brought closure to a decades-long cold case, largely driven by Davis's own public admissions and media interviews. This milestone has sparked questions and renewed interest regarding whether it could help inspire efforts to solve the similarly unsolved 1997 murder of Christopher Wallace, also known as Notorious B.I.G. While the LAPD states that Wallace's case remains an open and active investigation, no arrests have been made in that case.
key_points: Duane "Keffe D" Davis was convicted of the 1996 drive-by murder of rapper Tupac Shakur after prosecutors built a case largely using Davis's own admissions from documentaries, memoirs, and police interviews.
The successful prosecution of Shakur's murder has prompted observers to wonder if it could inspire renewed efforts to solve the unsolved 1997 murder of Notorious B.I.G. (Christopher Wallace).
Shakur and Wallace were central figures in the 1990s East Coast-West Coast hip-hop rivalry, and their murders shared similar drive-by shooting circumstances.
The LAPD stated that the investigation into Wallace's death remains an active, open, and unsolved case within its Robbery-Homicide Division.

title: Ex-LA gang leader found guilty of murdering Tupac Shakur
author: AFP; Reuters
content:
![32nd Annual Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony - Show – New York City, U.S., Alicia Keys performs in honor of the late Tupac Shakur.](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/2017-04-08T120000Z_1125167671_HP1ED48056WGP_RTRMADP_3_MUSIC-HALLOFFAME-1690451625.jpg?resize=730%2C410&quality=80)
Former gang leader found guilty of Tupac Shakur’s 1996 murder
A former gang leader accused of orchestrating the killing of hip-hop star Tupac Shakur in the United States in 1996 has been convicted of murder for his role in the long-unsolved crime.
A jury in Clark County, Nevada, deliberated for nearly three hours on Monday before finding Duane “Keffe D” Davis, 63, guilty of a single count of first-degree murder with a deadly weapon, capping an 11-day trial in a courtroom in the city of Las Vegas.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Suspect in rapper Tupac Shakur’s killing makes first court appearance in US
- list 2 of 4Who killed Tupac? What to know about the trial of Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis
- list 3 of 4‘Truth or fiction’: US trial of Tupac Shakur’s accused killer begins
- list 4 of 4Tupac Shakur murder trial begins thirty years after his death
Davis will face a maximum sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole at his sentencing on October 13. He told the judge “he plans to appeal this matter”.
Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips street gang in Los Angeles, was accused of ordering the drive-by shooting that killed Shakur on September 7, 1996. Prosecutors said he was enraged because members of Shakur’s entourage had beaten his nephew at a Las Vegas casino hours earlier.
“Duane Davis, in the culture of gangs, could not let that stand,” prosecutor Binu Palal said during closing arguments. “So what did he do? He acquired a firearm, got his group together and went hunting for Mr Shakur.”
Shakur, who was in Las Vegas for a Mike Tyson heavyweight fight, was shot about two hours after the casino confrontation by a gunman in a white Cadillac that pulled up at a red light alongside the BMW in which the rapper was riding in the front passenger seat.
According to prosecutors, Davis handed the gun to someone sitting in the back seat of the Cadillac and ordered that person to shoot Shakur, who died six days later.
Davis is the only person who was in the Cadillac that evening who is still alive.
The driver of the BMW, Death Row Records cofounder Marion “Suge” Knight, was wounded.
The killing of Shakur, also known as 2Pac, has been one of the US’s most notorious cold cases, prompting endless debate among music fans over who did it and why.
The investigation into Shakur’s murder sputtered for decades because of a lack of evidence, but the case was revived when Davis’s memoirs were published in 2019. Davis has repeatedly boasted over the years of involvement in Shakur’s murder, in interviews with law enforcement and media and ultimately in his autobiography, Compton Street Legend.
He has since backtracked and pleaded not guilty to the murder charge.
Palal, the prosecutor, played clips from Davis’s various alleged confessions as part of his closing arguments.
Michael Sanft, Davis’s defence attorney, characterised his client’s confessions as fiction and lies partly designed to promote his book.
“You’re reading a book that is fiction and not fact,” Sanft told the jury. “But the state wants you to believe that this is somehow a confession, that he was there and present at the time of the shooting.”
Sanft said there was no evidence implicating Davis in Shakur’s murder other than his own statements.
In the run-up to the trial, Davis’s lawyers tried in vain to keep the book from being introduced as evidence, along with remarks he made in an interview with police in 2008.
Shakur, who was 25 when he was killed, was a key figure in a hip-hop rivalry pitting US East Coast rappers against West Coast artists.
Known for hits including “California Love” and “All Eyez on Me”, Shakur – the son of a Black Panther – was raised in Harlem and Baltimore, but became the epitome of California hip-hop when he signed with Los Angeles-based Death Row Records.
summary: A Clark County, Nevada, jury has found former Los Angeles gang leader Duane "Keffe D" Davis guilty of first-degree murder with a deadly weapon for orchestrating the 1996 drive-by shooting of hip-hop star Tupac Shakur. Prosecutors argued that Davis sought revenge after Shakur's entourage beat his nephew at a Las Vegas casino hours prior to the attack. The long-unsolved cold case was revived largely due to statements Davis made in his 2019 memoir and various interviews, which the defense argued were mere fiction and lies to promote his book.
key_points: Duane "Keffe D" Davis was convicted of first-degree murder with a deadly weapon for the 1996 killing of Tupac Shakur.
Prosecutors stated that Davis orchestrated the drive-by shooting to avenge a casino beating his nephew suffered earlier that evening.
The decades-old cold case was revitalized after Davis detailed his involvement in media interviews and his 2019 autobiography.
Davis faces a maximum sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole, and his defense plans to appeal the conviction.

title: Duane "Keffe D" Davis found guilty in 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur
author: Anoushka Mutanda-Dougherty; Christal Hayes; Shaimaa Khalil; Regan Morris
content:
Watch: What it was like inside court for Tupac Shakurâs murder trial verdict
- Published
Former gang boss Duane "Keffe D" Davis has been found guilty of orchestrating the murder of Tupac Shakur - the first conviction in a cold case that has intrigued hip-hop fans for nearly 30 years.
The jury found Davis guilty of one count of murder with a deadly weapon for the rap superstar's death in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas on 7 September 1996.
Clad in a black suit, the 63-year-old stood impassively in the Las Vegas court as the verdict was read, before saying he would appeal. Shakur's relatives held hands, some hugging and crying.
Shakur was 25 when he was slain at the height of his career as one of rap's most influential voices. He has sold more than 75 million records worldwide.
![A man wears a black suit and patterned tie. He has a white goatee and serious expression.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/fdcd/live/2074f700-a5c6-11f1-8543-aba44f51f79c.jpg)
Duane Davis during closing arguments at court in Las Vegas
Prosecutors had argued during the trial that although Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips street gang, did not fire the gun that killed Shakur, he ordered the shooting and supplied the gun that his nephew Orlando Anderson used to open fire.
They told the court that Davis had planned the shooting as retaliation after Anderson was involved in a fight with Shakur and the rapper's crew in Las Vegas just hours earlier.
For 30 years, the case remained one of America's most famous cold cases, spurring countless conspiracies - but never a conviction, until now.
Shakur's murder happened at a time of intense rivalry between the East Coast and West Coast rap scene and amid gang feuds between the Bloods and Crips, which had deep roots within hip-hop at the time.
His family appeared emotional in court, his sister embracing a prosecutor after the verdict was read while others sat crying nearby.
Outside, devoted fans of Shakur were crying and cheering.
The key evidence in the case were Davis' own words, where he repeatedly and publicly acknowledged being inside the white Cadillac from where the deadly shots were fired.
He had told authorities about his role in Shakur's death during a secret 2008 police interview related to the death of fellow rapper Notorious B.I.G., real name Christopher Wallace.
Davis elaborated further on his role in his 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend.
But his book and media interviews voided a protective agreement he had established with authorities that had blocked any criminal charges being filed, with the court ruling his police interview could be used in the murder trial against him.
In closing arguments, prosecutor Binu Palal told jurors to take Davis at his word and find him guilty.
For years, he argued, Davis had been telling people "that he is responsible for Tupac Shakur's murder" through documentaries, his memoir, podcasts and a police interview.
"He's the shot caller - in every instance in every iteration he's the leader of the South Side Crips," Palal told the jury.
"When you have the shot caller sitting shotgun when shots are fired, there's no doubt he's responsible."
![A 1996 photo of rapper Tupac Shakur (L) and Marion "Suge" Knight displayed during the murder trial](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1504/cpsprodpb/fa9f/live/76b3ae70-a334-11f1-84e6-5f05e8e26a23.png)
A 1996 photo of rapper Tupac Shakur (L) and Marion "Suge" Knight displayed during the murder trial
Throughout the trial, Davis' defence team tried to persuade jurors that his comments were fiction - bravado and exaggeration intended to sell books and make money.
In closing arguments, his lawyer Michael Sanft urged the jury to discredit his client as a liar who just told tales to sell books.
"There's no proof," he told the jury.
But within hours of the jury being handed the case on Monday, they reached a guilty verdict.
Just before the court emptied out, Clark County District Court Judge Carli Kierny set Davis' sentencing for 13 October.
While reading out some procedural steps in the case, Davis appeared to interrupt by raising his hand.
"I would like my stuff," he told the judge, mentioning some personal items including his phone.
He continued: "I would like to appeal this matter."
The judge explained that this could happen after sentencing.
![A promo image shows Tupac and the words, "FAME UNDER FIRE THE TUPAC MURDER TRIAL"](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1536/cpsprodpb/e19b/live/4ecb7f70-a5bc-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.png)
summary: Former gang boss Duane "Keffe D" Davis has been found guilty of orchestrating the 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur in a Las Vegas drive-by shooting. The conviction marks the first time anyone has been held legally responsible in the nearly 30-year-old cold case. Prosecutors used Davis's own past statements, media interviews, and his 2019 memoir to prove he supplied the gun and acted as the shot caller, while the defense unsuccessfully argued his claims were merely fabricated stories to sell books.
key_points: Duane "Keffe D" Davis was found guilty of one count of murder with a deadly weapon for Tupac Shakur's 1996 death.
Prosecutors argued that Davis orchestrated the retaliation shooting and supplied the weapon used by his nephew, Orlando Anderson.
Key evidence included Davis's own public admissions, a 2008 police interview, and his 2019 memoir detailing his role.
The defense claimed Davis's public admissions were just fiction and bravado intended to make money and sell books.
Davis stated in court that he plans to appeal the verdict, and his sentencing is scheduled for 13 October.

title: Duane Keith Davis found guilty of 1996 murder of Tupac Shakur
author: Gabrielle Canon
content:
A Las Vegas jury has found former South Side Compton Crips gang leader Duane Keith Davis guilty of the murder of Tupac Shakur, bringing the case to a close nearly 30 years after the famous rapper was gunned down.
The jury took about three hours to reach a guilty verdict in a case that relied heavily on multiple confessions from Davis himself, including his description of the killing in the 2019 memoir Compton Street Legend.
Shakur was born in 1971 in East Harlem, New York, and rose to fame in the early nineties, with poetic flow that doubled as sharp commentary on social injustice, including systemic racism, police brutality and the struggles felt by marginalized communities.
![Tupac Shakur at the Premiere of I Like It Like That.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/959b4cc71ac0a3e010cb6bdc5ef5d63d21aad261/0_0_1946_3000/master/1946.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Regarded among the greatest rappers to ever live, Shakur affected generations and continued to be celebrated around the world even years after his life was cut short. He was only 25 years old when he died in the hospital days after being shot four times in a car near the Las Vegas Strip.
Reverence for the rapper has long inspired conspiracy theories about his death as questions swirled around who was involved, why the case remained open for years and even whether Shakur was actually dead.
The trial has offered some resolution, even as family members and fans continue to mourn both the man and the years it took to bring details of his death to light.
Over the weeks-long trial, Marc DiGiacomo, the Clark county district attorney, and Binu Palal, the chief deputy district attorney, brought 25 witnesses to the stand – including some who had to be ordered by the court because they were reluctant to testify – in their case against Davis.
The 63-year-old man who was accused of instigating the deadly shooting, although not pulling the trigger himself, had spent years telling investigators and interviewers alike of his direct involvement before he was arrested in 2023.
Davis’s attorney Michael Sanft tried to frame the stories and statements as the exaggerated and embellished claims of a man hoping to benefit from the public interest and unanswered questions around Shakur’s murder.
Prosecutors played eight hours of recordings, taken from four separate events in different years, during which Davis shared in his own words what happened the night of 7 September 1996. Davis wrote that he had hatched the plan to retaliate against Shakur, after the rapper’s entourage beat his nephew, Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, in the lobby of the MGM Grand earlier that night. Anderson, who died two years later in an unrelated shootout, was a member of a rival gang in Compton, California.
Shakur and the founder of his label, Marion “Suge” Knight, had attended a Mike Tyson boxing match at the casino when the altercation with Anderson took place, and were on their way to an after-party. A white Cadillac pulled up next to them while they were stopped at a red light, and someone in that car began shooting, according to investigators.
In his book, Davis claimed to have been in that car, and that he’d brought a .40-caliber Glock with him. “Them jumping on my nephew gave us the green light to want to do something to their ass,” he wrote. “Pac chose the wrong game to play.”
Tupac’s sister, Sekyiwa “Set” Shakur, cried as the verdict was read, while Davis’s son covered his face with his hand, according to the Associated Press.
“It was kinda hard for me to feel so happy at the same time knowing someone is going to jail for so long,” a teary-eyed Shakur fan named Jessica Martin told AP outside the courtroom. “But then I looked over at Tupac’s family and it reminded me of everything they’ve gone through. It’s really emotional.”
![Tupac Shakur and Marion Suge Knight, Death Row Records chair at a voter registration event in Los Angeles in 1996.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/024b70e00c95e81ef860415e9e0d35f0d897f339/0_0_3000_2550/master/3000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Clark county district court judge Carli Kierny scheduled Davis’s sentencing hearing for 13 October. Prosecutors had not sought the death penalty against Davis and, after the verdict, voluntarily dropped their efforts to tack a gang enhancement on to Davis’s conviction.
First-degree murder in Nevada carries penalties ranging from 20 years to life imprisonment. Davis said he plans to appeal the verdict.
While the trial has finally come to an end, family members had been left to wonder for years why it took so long for investigators to reach a conclusion in the case.
“We’ve been waiting 30 years to grieve properly,” Zayd Akinyela, Shakur’s cousin told reporters outside the courtroom when the trial was under way. “A lot of people don’t get to grieve until they understand what happened to their loved one and how it happened.”
A Los Angeles Times review of police missteps on the case, published in 2015, detailed how authorities failed to investigate Anderson even after details about the conflict between him and Shakur’s entourage became known. Police also declined to follow a lead from a member of Shakur’s entourage, who claimed he could identify the shooters. That witness died weeks later in a separate shooting, the Times reported.
The investigation highlighted why many of his followers, members of his family and Black leaders and entertainers have pointed to the case – and the years it took to reach a conclusion – as yet another indication of racism in a broken justice system.
Investigators, meanwhile, said it was challenging to prove because they struggled to produce physical evidence and faced strong resistance from potential witnesses, including other members of the rapper’s entourage. Even now, some resisted participating in the case and had to be compelled to come to court.
Davis ultimately became the prosecution’s lead witness, despite being the defendant. “Had he decided to never write the book,” DiGiacomo said during the trial, “he would not, probably, have ever been prosecuted for the crime.”
summary: A Las Vegas jury has found former gang leader Duane Keith Davis guilty of the 1996 murder of legendary rapper Tupac Shakur, bringing a nearly 30-year-old case to a close. The verdict relied heavily on Davis's own previous confessions, including statements made in his 2019 memoir describing his role in orchestrating the retaliation shooting. Davis, who did not pull the trigger himself but admitted to helping hatch the plan, faces sentencing in October and plans to appeal.
key_points: Duane Keith Davis was found guilty of the 1996 murder of Tupac Shakur by a Las Vegas jury.
The prosecution's case relied heavily on Davis's own past confessions, including details from his 2019 memoir.
The shooting was carried out to retaliate against Shakur after his entourage beat Davis's nephew earlier that night.
Davis's sentencing is scheduled for October, and he faces a prison sentence ranging from 20 years to life.

title: Dolly Parton laid to rest in private Nashville funeral
author: Owen Myers
content:
Dolly Parton was laid to rest in a private ceremony in Nashville on Friday, her family has confirmed.
The queen of country music, who died aged 80 on 25 August “after bravely facing a brief battle with cancer”, was interred at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum alongside her husband of 60 years, Carl Thomas.
Parton’s great-niece Lainey Parton wrote on Instagram on Saturday: “I wanted to wait until after my granny was laid to rest yesterday before I tried to put any of this into words.
“From the time I was little, my granny always had a way of making me feel like I was enough. She never made my dreams feel too big or made me feel like I couldn’t do something. She believed in me before I even knew how to believe in myself.
“Because she couldn’t have kids of her own, she always made us feel like we were hers,” Lainey continued. “She loved us that way, and I’ll forever be grateful for that.”
![Grave marker plaque](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/98df2697dd7311d4a48d3494b066ce27e71b6912/0_231_4376_3499/master/4376.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Only immediate family attended the small ceremony, People reported. Parton had her name engraved on the large mausoleum plaque at the cemetery before she died, as well as an engraving of the cabin in Sevier county, Tennessee, where she grew up.
On Saturday, Parton’s niece Jada Star took to the stage at Nashville’s Grand Ole Opry as part of a tribute concert to the country legend. Star performed a song titled The Orchard that she had recorded with Parton for her 2024 album Smoky Mountain DNA: Family, Faith and Fables.
In an Instagram post ahead of the performance, Star said, “I am walking around in a fog of sadness, like all of you have.
“I do not take this honor lightly. I will stand on that stage tonight, the stage she loved so much, and share my song I wrote for her and for my whole family.”
On Monday, the estate of Parton announced DollyFest, a two-weekend event which will take place in Nashville and London next year. Before her death, Parton had been planning the festival for January 2026 but had to take a step back due to health issues.
“As far as a traditional memorial goes, that is not something Dolly wanted,” said Parton’s manager, Danny Nozell, in a press release. “So, instead, it feels more appropriate for us to take a beat, let all the tributes that immediately make sense occur naturally, and then, see through this festival-style concept that was truly dreamed up by Dolly.”
![Woman performing on stage](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/049d77c4f2fce907ec6a6b36092ca4ad2ff06fed/342_0_4583_3667/master/4583.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Last week, Parton’s team confirmed that the projects she was working on before her death would continue to be brought to life, including a line of coffee grounds, a home decor collection and a Broadway musical to launch in New York later this year.
“Dolly worked up until the day she died,” Nozell said. “As the leader of the team responsible for overseeing her legacy, we will ensure the many dreams she had yet to fulfill are brought to life.”
Active projects that Parton was working on at the time of her death also include Dolly Parton’s SongTeller Hotel and Dolly’s Life of Many Colors Museum, which are both scheduled to open next month in Nashville. Meanwhile, Dolly Dolls and a range of Dolly’s Dog Treats are scheduled to be released in the coming months.
The family has asked for donations in Parton’s memory to be dedicated to Imagination Library, the organization she founded to encourage literacy and the love of reading in children.
summary: Country music icon Dolly Parton was laid to rest in a private ceremony in Nashville on Friday, attended by immediate family. Parton passed away at the age of 80 on August 25 following a brief battle with cancer. Rather than a traditional memorial, her estate plans to move forward with her previously conceived DollyFest event and continue her unfinished business and creative projects.
key_points: Dolly Parton was interred at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum alongside her late husband, Carl Thomas.
A tribute concert was held at Nashville's Grand Ole Opry featuring performances by her niece, Jada Star.
Her estate announced DollyFest, a two-weekend festival planned for next year in Nashville and London that Parton originally dreamed up.
Unfinished projects, including a Broadway musical, coffee line, hotel, and museum, will continue to be brought to life.
The family requested memorial donations be made to the Imagination Library literacy organization founded by Parton.

title: John Galliano exhibition at New York's Met cancelled after backlash
author: Ian Youngs
content:
![John Galliano attends The 2019 Met Gala Celebrating Camp: Notes on Fashion at Metropolitan Museum of Art on May 06, 2019 in New York City](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1376/cpsprodpb/87bf/live/7e3a5850-a547-11f1-8689-6589354d0f8e.jpg)
John Galliano said he realised "an exhibition honouring my work would be painful for some"
- Published
John Galliano has cancelled an upcoming major exhibition celebrating his work as a fashion designer after it prompted criticism due to his previous conviction for making antisemitic remarks.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York had announced an exhibition titled John Galliano: Horizons that was due to open in May 2027.
But Galliano said on Monday: "After much reflection and discussion with the Met and all those involved, I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time."
The British designer was sacked as creative director of Dior in 2011 and found guilty of abusing a Jewish curator in a restaurant in Paris.
A court also heard that he hurled racist insults at her friend, who is of South Asian origin, and in a separate incident declared a love for Hitler.
'I remain deeply sorry'
At the time, he apologised for his behaviour and his lawyer blamed it on "work-related stress and multiple addictions".
Galliano said in his statement on Monday: "I remain fully accountable for the pain caused by my words in the past, particularly the hurt I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities, and I remain deeply sorry for it.
"I understand that meaningful atonement is not achieved through an exhibition, institutional recognition or a single public gesture.
"It is a continuing responsibility, demonstrated through listening, learning and one's conduct over time."
Galliano added that he did not want "to distract from the remarkable work" of the Met's Costume Institute and said he recognised and respected that "an exhibition honouring my work would be painful for some".
Galliano's new statement noted his "15 years of sobriety and recovery from alcoholism and addiction".
![Anna Wintour in dark glasses and John Galliano in grey suit and black hat, seated together at a fashion show and looking expressionless at the camera](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/53f0/live/5f5b9870-a549-11f1-8689-6589354d0f8e.jpg)
Anna Wintour, pictured with Galliano in January, said he retained her "full support"
As well as being the focus of the exhibition, Galliano and his work in fashion would have provided the theme for the next Met Gala.
The star-studded event is due to take place on 3 May, coinciding with Yom HaShoah (Holocaust and Heroism Remembrance Day).
Vogue global editorial director Anna Wintour, a trustee of the Met and co-chair of the Met Gala, gave her support to Galliano on Monday.
"John's decision that the exhibition devoted to his work should not take place at this time is very courageous and a measure of the man he is," she said.
"I believe this is the right decision, and both he and the Museum have my full support."
'Misguided'
Others had previously voiced their opposition to the Met's plan to commemorate Galliano.
Julie Menin, speaker of New York City Council, said, external: "After my numerous and lengthy meetings and conversations with the Met, I am pleased that they have agreed to not honour John Galliano.
"From the beginning, I have told them that I strongly disagreed with this decision, and at this rising time of antisemitism, it had served as a gut punch to the Jewish community.
"This is the correct decision, as the harm and pain this was causing was simply unacceptable."
Meanwhile, Jonathan Greenblatt, chief executive of the Anti-Defamation League, which aims to counter antisemitism, said that with antisemitism at "crisis levels", honouring Galliano would be "misguided".
"Even Galliano ultimately recognised what the Met should have done from the start," he added. "This was the wrong move at the wrong moment. Timing matters."
Galliano is regarded by some as one of the greatest fashion designers and returned to the fashion industry following his conviction, serving as creative director of Margiela for a decade until 2024.
summary: Fashion designer John Galliano has cancelled a major retrospective exhibition at New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art following backlash over his 2011 conviction for antisemitic and racist remarks. The exhibition, titled John Galliano: Horizons, and the associated Met Gala had drawn strong criticism from community leaders due to the timing coinciding with Holocaust Remembrance Day and rising antisemitism. Galliano stated that he remains fully accountable for his past actions and agreed that honoring his work would be painful for some, while Vogue's Anna Wintour praised his decision.
key_points: John Galliano has cancelled his upcoming exhibition at the Metropolitan Museum of Art after facing criticism over his past antisemitic conviction.
The planned exhibition and Met Gala had drawn opposition from figures including New York City Council speaker Julie Menin and ADL chief executive Jonathan Greenblatt.
Galliano stated that he takes full responsibility for the pain caused by his past words and acknowledged that honoring his work would be painful for some.
Vogue global editorial director Anna Wintour expressed her full support for Galliano and his decision to call off the exhibition.

title: Dolly Parton laid to rest alongside husband in Nashville
author: Ian Youngs
content:
![More than two dozen singers and musicians in a row on stage below a large screen showing a photo of Dolly Parton and the Grand Ole Opry name](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/a59e/live/0255aa10-a519-11f1-89d5-dd5482a9fcc2.jpg)
A tribute concert was held at Nashville's Grand Ole Opry on Saturday
- Published
Dolly Parton has been laid to rest, the music legend's great-niece has said.
The singer had a private family funeral in Nashville on Friday, following her death earlier in the week at the age of 80.
She has been placed next to her late husband, Carl Dean, at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum in the Tennessee city.
Lainey Parton posted an emotional tribute, external a day after the burial, saying: "It still doesn't feel real that she's gone. I'm going to miss her voice, her laugh, her hugs, and just knowing she was there."
'She believed in me'
She referred to Parton as "granny" and wrote: "Because she couldn't have kids of her own, she always made us feel like we were hers. She loved us that way, and I'll forever be grateful for that."
Lainey remembered: "From the time I was little, my granny always had a way of making me feel like I was enough. She never made my dreams feel too big or made me feel like I couldn't do something. She believed in me before I even knew how to believe in myself."
Lainey also remembered how Parton had supported her through beauty school, explaining: "She didn't just tell me to chase my dreams, she helped me get there."
She thanked those who have sent messages and flowers.
"I feel incredibly lucky that I got to call her my granny," she added. "Thank you for always believing in me, loving me, and making me feel like I could do anything. I love you, Granny. Always."
![An illustration of Dolly Parton with her name stands on a table in front of a vase of pink lilies and behind three candles during the during a Seattle Community Vigil for Dolly Parton on Friday](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/339d/live/5b79cb30-a519-11f1-89d5-dd5482a9fcc2.jpg)
Candlelight vigils have been held in US cities including Seattle, where this tribute was placed
An obituary posted by Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum, external remembered "her timeless music and prolific songwriting, but also her wit, warmth, and kindness that made us all feel like family".
It continued: "Dolly Parton's legacy is one of love, kindness, and resilience. With a seven-decade career, she inspired multiple generations of artists and fans with her music and an unwavering commitment to making the world a better place."
It added: "In lieu of flowers, the family asks for donations to be made to Dolly Parton's Imagination Library." The Imagination Library was Parton's scheme to send free books to young children.
Amelia Young, a reporter for Nashville's NewsChannel 5, posted photos of flowers, external and a book of condolence at the tomb, which features a brass plaque showing Parton and Dean's names and engravings of their childhood homes.
![Jada Star on stage in front of the screen showing a photo of Dolly Parton](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/9436/live/d9a60e60-a519-11f1-89d5-dd5482a9fcc2.jpg)
Parton's niece Jada Star performed during the Grand Ole Opry tribute
On Saturday, one of Parton's nieces, Jada Star, performed as part of a tribute concert at Nashville's Grand Ole Opry House, regarded as the home of country music.
Star performed her song The Orchard, which she recorded with her aunt in 2024 on the album Smoky Mountain DNA: Family, Faith and Fables.
"I am walking around in a fog of sadness, like all of you have," Star posted before the performance alongside a broken heart emoji. "I do not take this honor lightly."
![Jelly Roll in black denim jacket and backwards black baseball cap, with one arm around Carly Pearce and the other holding a microphone and pointing in the air. Carly Pearce is weating a white lace dress and singing into her handheld microphone.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/1405/live/0e208120-a51a-11f1-89d5-dd5482a9fcc2.jpg)
Jelly Roll joined Carly Pearce during the tribute show
Country superstar Jelly Roll made a surprise appearance during the event's finale - a group performance of Parton's 9 to 5 - while other participants included Carly Pearce, who has gone from being a performer at Parton's Dollywood theme park to a Grammy-winning singer.
Meanwhile, Tennessee's governor has announced plans to name Nashville International Airport after Parton.
In the UK, 9 to 5 is on course to be number one in the singles chart this week, according to the Official Chart Company, after fans streamed it in big numbers following Parton's death.
However, its streaming numbers have begun to decline, meaning it may not remain in the number one spot when the final chart is announced on Friday.
- ![Dolly Parton](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/f552/live/798d9880-a32b-11f1-8e46-c39d9fc92d9e.jpg)
- ![Dolly Parton strums a guitar while looking to the right of frame wearing a blue top against a background of wooden panels on ABC TV in 1987.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/ede3/live/8fa98930-a10f-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
  - Published5 days ago
 ![Dolly Parton smiling for the cameras while wearing a white sequined outfit at the Hollywood premiere of Joyful Noise in Los Angeles in 2012](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/bdeb/live/f73e1300-a11d-11f1-92eb-a9b3bbcf6f4a.jpg)
summary: Music legend Dolly Parton has been laid to rest next to her late husband, Carl Dean, at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum in Nashville following a private family funeral. Parton passed away earlier in the week at the age of 80, prompting tributes from family members, candlelight vigils across US cities, and a tribute concert at the Grand Ole Opry. Additionally, Tennessee's governor announced plans to name Nashville International Airport after Parton.
key_points: Dolly Parton was laid to rest at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum next to her late husband, Carl Dean.
A tribute concert was held at Nashville's Grand Ole Opry featuring performances by her niece Jada Star and other artists.
The family requested that donations be made to Dolly Parton's Imagination Library in lieu of flowers.
Tennessee's governor announced plans to name Nashville International Airport after Parton.

title: Original Days of Thunder star rails against Anne Hathaway casting: ‘Horrible choice’
author: Caitlin Hornik
content:
When the Days of Thunder follow up film was announced Saturday by Tom Cruise and Anne Hathaway, many fans were thrilled — with one notable exception.
Randy Quaid, who starred with Cruise in the original 1990 Nascar film, ranted about Hathaway’s casting in a post on X.
“Anne Hathaway is a leftist, woke, horrible choice for DAYS OF THUNDER NASCAR audience who are MAGA,” Quaid began.
“The sexy older chick for Tom in this film needs to be Nicole,” he continued, likely referring to Nicole Kidman who starred in the original film.
“That’s the casting that would sell the idea. It’s interesting because when we made the first one there was also a rush to get it out; editors slept in the cutting room on shifts. This is a weird thing, like they want it to come out and tank.”
![Randy Quaid has railed against the forthcoming ‘Days of Thunder’ film](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/30/16/18/Randy-Quaid.png)
In a separate post, Quaid again advocated for Kidman’s casting while railing against Hathaway and Cruise, writing: “We need Nicole back. Don’t be a p***y, @TomCruise. You need the original girl. It’s not personal; it’s filmmaking. Anne isn’t sexy, because and if you haven’t noticed, she’s pregnant.”
And in yet another post, he wrote: “If I were in control of production, a real sequel worth watching for DAYS OF THUNDER would be seeing Tom and Nicole together on screen again. We don’t need a new girl; we need a new race car!”
The Independent has contacted representatives for Cruise and Hathaway for comment.
Hathaway is one of the most in-demand stars in Hollywood, with four films out already this year and another — Verity, the latest film adaptation from author Colleen Hoover — slated for an October release.
![Tom Cruise and Anne Hathaway are teaming up for a 'Days of Thunder' follow up film](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/30/16/01M17JKWZ805EMCPCZ3M38DBHZ.jpg)
An Oscar winner for the 2012 film adaptation of Les Misérables, Hathaway is also pregnant with her third child. She confirmed in the announcement for the Days of Thunder sequel that she’ll give birth before filming commences.
Hathaway and Cruise will film the sequel nearly 40 years after the original movie was released. The new film is slated for a June 2028 release.
According to Variety, Cruise will reprise his role from the first film as Cole Trickle. Hathaway will play a racecar team owner and engineer. Jonathan Levine will direct, and Cruise will produce alongside Jerry Bruckheimer and Tommy Harper.
In addition to Cruise, the original Days of Thunder starred Kidman, Quaid, Robert Duvall and John C. Reilly. It is not yet clear whether any of the original cast will return for the follow up. Duvall died earlier this year.
summary: Original Days of Thunder star Randy Quaid criticized the casting of Anne Hathaway in the upcoming sequel on social media. Quaid argued that Tom Cruise should reunite with his original co-star, Nicole Kidman, instead of Hathaway. Cruise and Hathaway are set to star in the follow-up film directed by Jonathan Levine, scheduled for a June 2028 release.
key_points: Randy Quaid publicly criticized Anne Hathaway's casting in the Days of Thunder sequel on X.
Quaid advocated for Nicole Kidman to return as Tom Cruise's love interest instead of Hathaway.
Tom Cruise will reprise his role as Cole Trickle, while Hathaway will play a racecar team owner and engineer.
The sequel is directed by Jonathan Levine and slated for a June 2028 release.

title: Vigil recaptures its mojo in the Arctic
author: Benji Wilson
content:
![Rose Leslie and Suranne Jones head to the Arctic for the third series of the BBC thriller](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/tv/2026/08/27/TELEMMGLPICT000499698708_17878301203520_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqMNWpgD2PZIvlOBIGuRStEyqVm7pDLexZy36ab3xAREw.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Rose Leslie and Suranne Jones head to the Arctic for the third series of the BBC thriller](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/tv/2026/08/27/TELEMMGLPICT000499698708_17878301203520_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqMNWpgD2PZIvlOBIGuRStEyqVm7pDLexZy36ab3xAREw.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
The first series of Vigil (BBC One) was set on a submarine and was very good, precisely because it was set on a submarine. A disparate group of sailors cooped up for months, going loco and killing each other – what’s not to like? The second series, two years later, widened its horizons and lost its mojo. It was all about drones and, true to its subject, felt like it went on a bit. For series three, therefore, Tom Edge, the writer, has tried to replicate the sardine-can sense of isolation and dread from series one by transplanting the whole thing to remotest Svalbard, Norway.
Once again, we get the dynamic duo of Amy Silva (Suranne Jones) and Kirsten Longacre (Rose Leslie), who in episode one are summoned to a remote Arctic research station after a tough nut in a covert British special forces mission is shot dead. Needless to say, this one goes right to the very top, as conspiracy thrillers always do. (As an aside, I long for a thriller whose big reveal is that it doesn’t go to the very top, and is just a miscreant doing something silly at the very bottom that is solved by a junior detective in 25 minutes and doesn’t involve bald men in navy suits barking: “Just get it done!” into secure phones).
![tmg.video.placeholder.alt t2GzDAN1q2A](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/t2GzDAN1q2A/maxresdefault.jpg) 
The plus points of an Arctic setting are the aforementioned stir-craziness and the fact that everyone has to carry a high-powered rifle around in case they bump into a polar bear. All of the ingredients for seemingly random killings are right there. The downside is that screenwriters have noticed this already: both 2015’s Fortitude and 2024’s True Detective: Night Country used strange happenings at distant research stations conducting controversial environmental studies as their jumping-off points.
Not that you’d ever get bored of glaciers and long horizons, but it does mean that Vigil series three has to work for exciting incidents. The show throws Russians, Chinese, spies, special forces, eco-terrorists, the fossil-fuel disaster and the completely impossible task of politicians trying to work through all of the above into the mix.
The task facing the producers of a drama like this one is to tip-toe down the tightrope of implausibility while holding the balancing pole of the feasible. Vigil gets it just about right, asking pertinent questions about the climate emergency without lecturing, while still allowing itself the luxury of imagining that someone is coming to fix things.
![The show manages to  tip-toe down the tightrope of implausibility](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/tv/2026/08/27/TELEMMGLPICT000499024504_17878299632870_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
But it does suffer from the old X-Files problem of “trust no one”, It’s one thing for Silva and Longacre to be asking themselves who they can trust (answer: no one), but there’s the further issue of who the viewer can trust. We know now in conspiracy thrillers that the nameless nice guys are most often the wrong’uns, but we still need to feel that the writers have interests at heart other than just getting us to the next episode.
On this count, Vigil broadly succeeds, because its central characters are credible and well played. You stick with the show, as daft as it sometimes gets, because you want to stick with its leading ladies. Ultimately, in a world full of liars, they’re just trying to work out what’s the right thing to do and how to do it. Buy that, and you’ll follow them all the way to Svalbard and back.
Vigil is on BBC One at 9pm on Sunday, Aug 30, and BBC iPlayer
summary: The third series of the BBC thriller Vigil relocates its action to a remote Arctic research station in Svalbard, Norway, aiming to recapture the isolated atmosphere of the first season. Detectives Amy Silva and Kirsten Longacre return to investigate the murder of a British special forces member in a plot involving international espionage and environmental issues. Despite familiar conspiracy tropes, the show succeeds largely due to the credible and well-played performances of its leading actresses.
key_points: Series three of Vigil is set in remotest Svalbard, Norway, to replicate the isolated atmosphere of the first season.
Suranne Jones and Rose Leslie return as dynamic duo Amy Silva and Kirsten Longacre.
The plot begins with the murder of a covert British special forces operative at an Arctic research station.
The narrative incorporates complex elements including international spies, eco-terrorists, and the climate emergency.
The show maintains viewer engagement primarily through the credible performances of its central characters.

title: Reading Festival: Messy singer Lola Young makes surprise final day appearance
author: Adam Goldsmith
content:
![Singer Lola Young is pictured on stage at the Reading music festival. She is smiling while holding a microphone. She is wearing a black top with a tartan trim.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/699/cpsprodpb/0fc2/live/5d0d2160-a495-11f1-8395-fb1eae51ae18.jpg)
- Published
Fans at the final day of Reading Festival were treated to a surprise set from singer Lola Young.
"I am backstage, the cat is out of the bag and I am going to be performing so see you... at the Grid stage," she teased on Instagram, before treating fans to hits including number one single Messy and One Thing.
Her performance marks the latest step in a return to the spotlight after she had to cancel a string of shows last year following an on-stage collapse in September.
Young also pulled out of the 2025 Reading festival due to a scheduling clash.
The weekend festival concludes on Sunday with a line-up including performances by drum and bass duo Chase & Status, and Florence + The Machine.
After Charli XCX ushered in her own new era with an electrifying set following her latest release Music, Fashion, Film, Young's return was welcomed by festival-goers in Reading on Sunday.
Young had cancelled her scheduled appearance at Reading Festival last year due to an "unavoidable scheduling conflict".
A month later, Young dropped her microphone, collapsed backwards and had to be helped off stage in front of a festival crowd in New York.
A few days later, she cancelled all shows "for the foreseeable future".
"I really hope you'll give me a second chance once I've had some time to work on myself and come back stronger," she posted in a message to fans at the time.
Young has sought treatment for drug dependency and told the Guardian, external in 2025 that addiction had dogged her for "a long time".
The pop star has since returned to performing with a small run of shows in the UK, starting with a London gig in March.
"It felt so right being back on stage," she wrote on social media shortly after, but said: "As tempting as it is to jump on a big tour I'm going to continue taking things slowly despite feeling so ready to perform more."
Before touching down in Reading, Young performed at the Electric Picnic Festival in the Republic of Ireland on Saturday.
Although she has returned to performing and released reflective single From Down Here in May this year, fans are still awaiting a fourth album.
Reading Festival winds down on Sunday night with a star-studded cast including indie icon Florence and the Machine, R&B hit-maker Loyle Carner, and Irish rap group Kneecap.
The festival's other site in Leeds, meanwhile, closes after performances from singer-songwriter Raye and multi award-winning rapper Dave on Sunday night.
![Lola Young on stage in green trousers and a black top](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/998/cpsprodpb/61bb/live/f61c1e00-a49b-11f1-837c-8514728b4183.jpg)
- ![A black and white photo of Charli XCX leaning against a wall as she sings into a microphone. There is a bright white wall behind her which silhouettes her body.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/86ea/live/35df52c0-a32d-11f1-8e46-c39d9fc92d9e.jpg)
  - Published5 March
 ![Lola young on stage playing an acoustic guitar and singing into a microphone](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/e0f0/live/87b385e0-186c-11f1-8f1d-d7bdb1ea156f.jpg)
  - Published2 days ago
 ![Crowds of festival-goers wave their hands in the air at Leeds Festival. There a few people in the crowd raised up by sitting on the shoulders of other people.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/5d84/live/c30d5820-a249-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
summary: Singer Lola Young made a surprise appearance on the final day of the Reading Festival, performing hits including her number one single Messy on the Grid stage. This performance marks a continuation of her return to the spotlight after she cancelled shows last year following an on-stage collapse and treatment for drug dependency. Young previously missed out on festival appearances due to scheduling clashes and health reasons, but she has recently begun a gradual return to live performing.
key_points: Lola Young delivered a surprise set on the final day of the Reading Festival.
She performed hits like Messy and One Thing on the Grid stage.
The performance is part of her gradual return to the stage following an on-stage collapse and treatment for drug dependency last year.
Prior to Reading, she performed at the Electric Picnic Festival in Ireland.

title: Dame Meera Syal reveals she was sexually assaulted in her 20s
author: Telegraph Reporters
content:
![Meera Syal](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/30/TELEMMGLPICT000488196045_17880985246050_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwauLYewjGO21NF-o1gxbkUI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Meera Syal](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/30/TELEMMGLPICT000488196045_17880985246050_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwauLYewjGO21NF-o1gxbkUI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Dame Meera Syal has said she was sexually assaulted in her 20s, an experience she said had “completely changed my life”.
The 65-year-old actress rose to fame after co-creating and starring in the hit sketch comedy series Goodness Gracious Me, and later appearing in its spin-off The Kumars at No 42.
She has now spoken publicly about being attacked by an older man she thought she could trust until he tried to rape her.
The sexual assault, which happened in the 1980s, was never reported because Dame Meera could not bear the thought of putting her parents through a criminal trial. She told no one at the time.
Speaking to The Times, she said: “This is the first time I’ve spoken about this publicly. It completely changed my life and the direction of my career. I could have given up, but instead I sought out a group of South Asian writers.
“They encouraged me to write more, they found me a place to live, they healed me and awakened me politically.”
Writing strong female characters
Years later, she opened up to a group of friends and learnt that many of them had endured something similar.
Dame Meera said the assault led her to write the strong female characters that have featured in the acclaimed BBC sketch show and other comedy shows that changed her life.
Speaking about the sitcom Goodness Gracious Me, in which her husband, Sanjeev Bhaskar, also starred, she said: “It was a golden age of sketch comedy, alternative comedy and Cool Britannia. There was a real embracing of multicultural Britain. How times have changed.”
Dame Meera said the current political climate is giving her a “horrible sense of deja vu” specifically around immigration. She described how, when growing up, the initials of the far-Right National Front party were painted on her house.
She added: “Some people who feel hard done by need to be listened to, but their frustration is being weaponised and exploited by certain public figures against immigrants.”
Despite her decades-long career, Dame Meera said she does not “glide in and out of jobs” and believes “there still aren’t that many good roles for older women”. Speaking about what her dream role would be, she said: “A badass godmother, head of a clan or a crime syndicate.
“If you had met some of the badass aunties I have met you would know they could run that ship without blinking. And she would be called something you wouldn’t expect, like Sweetie Auntie.”
summary: Dame Meera Syal has publicly revealed for the first time that she was sexually assaulted by an older man in the 1980s when she was in her 20s. She did not report the attack at the time to spare her parents a criminal trial, but the experience ultimately shaped her career and inspired her to write strong female characters. In a recent interview, she also discussed her decades-long acting career, the political climate surrounding immigration, and the scarcity of good roles for older women.
key_points: Dame Meera Syal revealed she was sexually assaulted in her 20s by an older man she thought she could trust.
The 1980s assault was never reported because she did not want to put her parents through a criminal trial.
The experience influenced the direction of her career and inspired her to write strong female characters.
She expressed concern that the current political climate regarding immigration creates a sense of deja vu.
She noted that a lack of good roles for older women persists in the industry.

title: Dolly, inc: How the Queen of Country built her business empire
author: James Hall
content:
![American singer and songwriter Dolly Parton poses for a portrait at Dollywood on October 24, 1988 in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee.](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000499593342_178774882943617_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqbVGIJc7U-PZBMr9f92rSpGwWMIa6ROzpVxfgVoPIevI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![American singer and songwriter Dolly Parton poses for a portrait at Dollywood on October 24, 1988 in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee.](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000499593342_178774882943617_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqbVGIJc7U-PZBMr9f92rSpGwWMIa6ROzpVxfgVoPIevI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Dolly Parton, who has died aged 80, will be remembered best for her music. But the country star also ran an astonishing business and entertainment empire that took in everything from theme parks and hit films to clothing for dogs. While most of us were tumbling out of bed and stumbling to the kitchen of a morning, the indefatigable Parton was no doubt already up to keep a close eye on the myriad enterprises that made up Dolly, inc.
“I work my butt off,” the 9 to 5 hitmaker told Bloomberg in a 2024 interview. And her entrepreneurial flair was not restricted to selling rollercoaster rides or rhinestone-encrusted “stuff”. Parton was a trailblazer when it came to owning the rights to her own music and, perhaps incongruously for a musician, helping scientists develop a Covid vaccine during the 2020 pandemic. It’s little wonder that Parton’s net worth has been valued at between $440m and $650m (£340m to £485m).
Parton’s best known business venture is Dollywood, the 160-acre theme park in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, where a two-day adult ticket starts at $125 (£95). Opened in 1986, Dollywood offers visitors more than 50 rides, ranging from the Dollywood Express – a coal-fired steam train that takes people on a five-mile trip through the foothills of the Great Smoky Mountains – to the Tennessee Tornado – a 70mph big dipper. Dollywood also houses theatres, blacksmithery and glass-blowing workshops, and the Dolly Parton Experience, a multi-building tribute to the singer that includes the “Behind the Seams” exhibition about her clothing.
![Photo of COUNTRY & WESTERN and DOLLYWOOD and Dolly PARTON and COUNTRY](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000499593344_178774882920215_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqBmo3ZBPOSwC7GqRZsuXAwCTc4m2O3CKB7TalllG6rcY.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Also under the Dollywood umbrella sit the Splash Country water park, a horse-based show called Dolly Parton’s Stampede Dinner Attraction and two Dollywood spa resorts. At one of these resorts you can stay in the lavishly upholstered “Gypsy Wagon” tour bus that transported Parton for 360,000 miles across North America between 2008 and 2022. The bus comes with a bath, a wig cabinet, a full-size fridge and hand-painted murals on the walls (a two-night-minimum stay for two people starts at $10,000 (£7,500), with profit going to The Dollywood Foundation). In September, Dolly Parton’s SongTeller Hotel is opening in Nashville. The 245-room hotel, which also contains two live music venues, is her “love letter to the city”, she said.
![In September, Dolly Parton's SongTeller Hotel is due to open in Nashville](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/music/2026/08/28/TELEMMGLPICT000499800537_17879120657880_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwSX5rhseiWKOo9p9OQ-ymek.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
As with most of Parton’s business enterprises, Dollywood is run as a joint venture with a large corporation. In this case it’s Herschend Family Entertainment, the theme park behemoth that also owns the Harlem Globetrotters basketball team. Describing Dollywood earlier this year in a statement to celebrate it being voted America’s favourite theme park by the National Amusement Park Historical Association (above the likes of Disneyland), Herschend said the place “isn’t just a theme park. It’s a love letter to East Tennessee”. Its three million visitors a year clearly agree.
Then there are the TV and film successes. Parton’s production company Sandollar was behind the 1991 Steve Martin hit film Father of the Bride (which grossed $89m at the box office on a $20m budget) and the hugely popular TV show Buffy the Vampire Slayer starring Sarah Michelle Gellar (and also the Buffy spinoff series, Angel). Sandollar was another joint venture, this time with Parton’s former manager Sandy Gallin. The company has gone through various iterations and is now called Dixie Pixie Productions.
Parton’s business ventures wouldn’t have been complete without some high kitsch. In 2022 she launched Doggy Parton, a clothing and accessories line for pooches that included mini cowboy hats, wigs and gingham dresses “with a little Dolly flair”. She also wrote a series of picture books, including a number about a French Bulldog called Billy the Kid. Food featured heavily in her business interests too: she had ranges of branded frozen meals, desserts and baking products. A single box of her sweet cornbread and muffin mix, launched in conjunction with food company Duncan Hines, costs $2.87 at Walmart. The pink packet is dominated by a portrait of Parton – her voluminous golden locks take up almost as much space as the picture of the similarly coloured cornbread.
!['A little Dolly flair': Doggy Parton is a clothing and accessories line for dogs](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000499594252_17877488282063_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqAHSO9YcRn5Jrj-vTPE9vj4pXWSGeG3wfTcFmoZLWsNI.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
![Dolly Parton Duncan Hines food products](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000499594372_17877488269581_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqRo0U4xU-30oDveS4pXV-Vv4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Parton readily admitted that her strengths lay in songwriting and performing, so her trick was to cede business decisions to experts. “I just try to put people that are smarter than me in all the right places, and then I go on about my business,” she told Bloomberg. “I’m more of the creative force. I try to find the best people, and I try to trust them to do what they say they can do. Then I have people looking out after all of them.”
One area where she was consistently ruthless was around her songwriting royalties. Parton owned the publishing copyright for nearly all her song catalogue. This stemmed from a strategically smart decision she made back in 1966, aged just 20. When her music publishing contract with a company called Combine Music expired, Parton and her musician uncle Bill Owens founded their own company called Owe-Par Publishing, which meant they could keep the copyright for their songs. Crucially, Parton had a controlling share in Owe-Par. Such deals are increasingly commonplace in music today but back then they were almost unheard of. Over her career Parton estimated she’d written close to 3,000 songs.
As well as writing tracks for herself, her songs were covered by other artists including Tina Turner (1974’s There’ll Always Be Music) and Emmylou Harris (To Daddy, 1977). And with Parton’s own catalogue including Jolene and 9 to 5 (a combined 1.6 billion Spotify streams and counting), the royalties rolled in. Nowhere was this more apparent with I Will Always Love You, which Parton wrote and recorded in 1973.
A hit for Parton in its own right, I Will Always Love You piqued the interest of Elvis Presley, who wanted to cover it in 1974. However it came with a catch: Presley’s manager Colonel Tom Parker told Parton that she’d have to sign over half the publishing rights to Elvis. The steely Parton refused, crying all night that she’d turned down The King. But vindication came when Whitney Houston’s 1992 power-ballad version of the song, from the film The Bodyguard, was number one for 14 weeks in the US and 10 weeks in the UK.
Parton made a reported $20m (£15m) in royalties from Houston’s hit. “When Whitney’s [version] came out, I made enough money to buy Graceland,” Parton wryly told country-music TV channel CMT. According to Business Insider, Parton’s music catalogue earned her royalties of $6 to $8m a year. Taylor Swift is one of the artists who walked through the gate that Parton kicked open when it comes to owning the publishing rights to her songs.
But Dolly, inc wasn’t just about making money. It was about giving it away, too. We tend to equate philanthropy with virtue-signalling in this country. But it’s seen differently in America – and, boy, did Parton make a difference through The Dollywood Foundation, which is funded from her profits.
Her Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library mails one book a month to millions of children around the world from the day they’re born until they’re 5. One in seven children under the age of 5 in the US now receives a monthly book. In 2008, the scheme launched in the UK, where six million books have since been distributed. The fact that Parton launched the Library in honour of her father, who could neither read nor write, adds to its poignancy. Elsewhere, Parton has regularly donated millions of dollars to hospitals and victims of natural disasters, as well as campaigning to preserve the bald eagle when its status was threatened. Some profits from Doggy Parton went to a pet rescue centre. But perhaps Parton’s most notable contribution to public life came during the Covid pandemic.
When Covid struck, Parton donated $1m towards research at Vanderbilt University Medical Centre in Nashville. The donation helped fund the early stages of development of the Moderna vaccine. In March 2021, Parton became one of the first people to be vaccinated with a Moderna shot. “Dolly gets a dose of her own medicine,” she wrote on social media. Before she was injected she sang an adapted version of Jolene: “Vaccine, vaccine, vaccine… I’m begging you, please don’t hesitate / Vaccine, vaccine… Because once you’re dead, then that’s a bit too late.” The following month, the UK government bought 17 million doses of Moderna, enough to vaccinate 8.5 million people.
![Dolly Parton receives a vaccination against the coronavirus disease (COVID-19) at Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville, Tennessee](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000252360260_178774882852822_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqwtUT54c80eKHJHMfvK9NIl5NUcTKNHKqy85KLqtvPLE.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Dame Kate Bingham, who chaired the UK Vaccine Taskforce, is in little doubt about the role that Parton played. “Dolly Parton’s donation to Vanderbilt helped fund the early immunology work that confirmed the Moderna vaccine produced a protective immune response – a vital step in the discovery of one of the Covid vaccines that ended the pandemic,” Bingham tells me. “Her timely investment in discovery research paid huge dividends for people all over the world. Leadership in science comes in many forms, not just from the lab bench.”
Parton’s cup of ambition knew no bounds.
summary: Dolly Parton built an extensive business and entertainment empire alongside her legendary music career, encompassing theme parks, production companies, hotels, and various consumer products. She was a trailblazer in retaining her music publishing rights, generating millions in royalties while refusing unfavorable deals like Elvis Presley's offer. Furthermore, Parton used her wealth for extensive philanthropy, funding literacy programs, natural disaster relief, and even contributing to early Covid-19 vaccine research.
key_points: Parton co-founded Owe-Par Publishing in 1966 to maintain a controlling share of her music copyrights, earning millions annually in royalties.
Her best-known venture is the 160-acre Dollywood theme park in Tennessee, operated as a joint venture with Herschend Family Entertainment.
Her production company, Sandollar (now Dixie Pixie Productions), worked on successful films and television shows like Father of the Bride and Buffy the Vampire Slayer.
Through The Dollywood Foundation, she established the Imagination Library, which mails free books monthly to millions of children worldwide.
Parton donated $1 million to Vanderbilt University Medical Center to support early research for the Moderna Covid-19 vaccine.

title: Bill Maher makes sour comment about Dolly Parton’s death
author: Roisin O'Connor
content:
