Grint previously originated the film role of Ron Weasley across all eight Harry Potter movies.
Tom Felton was the first original film actor to join the stage production as Draco Malfoy, resulting in record-breaking box office grosses for the show.
Grint's return to Broadway marks his first appearance there in over a decade, following his 2014 debut in "It's Only a Play."

title: Tim Curry, star of The Rocky Horror Picture Show and Stephen King’s It, dies aged 80
author: Andrew Pulver
content:
Tim Curry, the versatile performer of screen and stage, who made his name as the flamboyant Dr Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Show, has died aged 80. Reports say Curry died at his home in Los Angeles.
Ironically, Curry’s best-known roles all required a considerable physical transformation, to the extent that he was unrecognisable in all of them. Frank-N-Furter, Rocky Horror’s deranged scientist, saw him daubed in garish makeup and wearing stockings and suspenders, for the stage show (which debuted in 1973) and the film adaptation (released in 1975). In the Ridley Scott-directed fantasy Legend (1985), he was equipped with giant horns and scarlet skin as the Lord of Darkness. And in 1990, Curry was transformed with full-face clown pancake to play Pennywise in the TV miniseries It, based on the Stephen King novel.
![Curry in heavy makeup, a black basque, stockings and suspenders.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/static/sys-images/Guardian/Pix/pictures/2015/11/11/1447240700670/b3bf719a-ceb6-4fbd-a84d-7692fe555646-2060x1236.jpeg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Alongside these show-stopping incarnations, Curry enjoyed a successful parallel career in film, TV and theatre. Born in 1946, he earned a degree in drama and English from the University of Birmingham in 1968 and embarked on a stage career. His first significant role was in the original cast for the first West End production of the controversial musical Hair, in 1968 – where he met Richard O’Brien, who would go on to cast him in his own musical, The Rocky Horror Show. Curry went on to play Tristan Tzara in Tom Stoppard’s Travesties (taking over the role from John Hurt and Robert Powell), and Mozart in the Broadway transfer of Amadeus in 1980. Later highlights included King Arthur in the Broadway run of the Monty Python musical Spamalot.
![Curry in clown face makeup and red hair.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/static/sys-images/Guardian/Pix/pictures/2015/11/11/1447240844521/abe0b9ef-9a1d-4608-a017-dc2eb8fa49ad-1020x612.jpeg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Curry worked regularly in film, in roles including that of Robert Graves in Jerzy Skolimowski’s sinister The Shout, and later as Jeremy in the Ian McEwan-scripted political drama The Ploughman’s Lunch. Later, Curry found himself working largely in comedies – including Home Alone 2: Lost in New York, Muppet Treasure Island, Scary Movie 2, and McHale’s Navy – before providing voiceovers for numerous animated films, such as Garfield: A Tail of Two Kitties, A Turtle’s Tale: Sammy’s Adventures and Ribbit.
Curry was also a regular presence on TV for more than four decades, playing William Shakespeare in John Mortimer’s six-part biography of the playwright in 1978, Bill Sikes in the 1982 US TV adaptation of Oliver Twist, and the wizard Trymon in the adaptation of Terry Pratchett’s The Colour of Magic in 2008. He voiced a stream of animated series (Duckman, Sonic the Hedgehog, The Mask and Star Wars: The Clone Wars) and was cast in many guest roles in established series, including Psych, Poirot and Criminal Minds.
“I’ve had the opportunities,” he said to the Guardian in 2025, “and I’m still showing up. You know? I think that’s what you have to do. You have to keep showing up.”
In 2012, Curry had a stroke while receiving a massage and received brain surgery. He was left with mobility issues and his short-term memory was also affected. “It was an odd thing, because my father had a stroke and died very soon afterwards,” he said. “I knew I had to force myself to relax and just take the opportunity to float a little.”
In 2025, he released his memoir Vagabond.
“I’m very aware that I’m lucky,” Curry said last year. “I’m astonished actually at how ambitious I’ve been. I didn’t think of myself as ambitious at all.”
summary: Tim Curry, the versatile screen and stage performer renowned for his role as Dr Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Show, has died at the age of 80 at his Los Angeles home. Throughout his extensive career, he became famous for transformative physical roles, including the Lord of Darkness in Legend and Pennywise in the miniseries It. Alongside his iconic film and television work, Curry enjoyed a prolific career in theatre, comedies, voiceovers, and later released his memoir Vagabond in 2025.
key_points: Tim Curry passed away at his home in Los Angeles at the age of 80.
He was best known for major physical transformations in roles such as Dr Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Picture Show and Pennywise in Stephen King's It.
His career spanned decades across stage productions, feature films, television, comedies, and voice acting for animated series.
He suffered a stroke in 2012 that left him with mobility issues and affected his short-term memory.
In 2025, Curry released his memoir titled Vagabond.

title: Harry and Meghan land in Britain
author: Hannah Furness
content:
![The Sussexes landed at Birmingham Airport at lunchtime on Wednesday](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/royal-family/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000499589845_17877451933760_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq-cVLixJZjJiTSS6NRQsYH3wSCF1R0VweJ7DS2UnVMSQ.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![The Sussexes landed at Birmingham Airport at lunchtime on Wednesday](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/royal-family/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000499589845_17877451933760_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq-cVLixJZjJiTSS6NRQsYH3wSCF1R0VweJ7DS2UnVMSQ.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have landed in Britain, ready to begin an “extended stay” with their children.
The Sussexes landed at Birmingham Airport at lunchtime on Wednesday.
Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, will start at a British school next week, at the start of the autumn term.
The family made a short visit to Britain in July for a summer holiday, with the Duchess sharing photographs of their time at Althorp on her Instagram page.
![The Duchess posted on Instagram pictures of Prince Harry and the children at the Althorp estate](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/royal-family/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000496219368_17877338450660_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqG5EXgvdXl1oBhJJqank9JMwZgCewa-xkrckcIXHk6m8.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The Duke and Duchess are moving to Britain six years after they left the working Royal family. Their UK home is thought to be in the Cotswolds.
They plan to live as an “international” family, keeping their homes in California and Portugal.
A source told The Telegraph: “How long will they stay? I don’t know, but it will be for an extended period. Whether that’s six months, a year, two years… who knows.”
The couple are bringing their dogs Mia and Pula with them, but are keeping their chickens in Montecito rather than rehoming them, suggesting they plan to return.
The Duke and Duchess will not resume their pre-2020 roles as working members of the Royal family in Britain.
![Duke and Duchess](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000499564657_17877229551950_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwVVuduJKBIVmdsWxwOVYZQY.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
While their allies have signalled that the Sussexes hope to be “half-in, half-out”, in the model of their tour of Australia earlier this year, the King and Prince of Wales are said to be united in upholding the terms of the Sandringham summit.
Then, Elizabeth II ruled that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex could not adopt a part-time working role in the Royal family while also making money in the way they had proposed.
The King and Queen hosted the Duke and Duchess, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, for tea at Highgrove in July.
The meeting was said to have gone well, but details of what was said between father and son have not yet been revealed.
The Prince of Wales and the Duke of Sussex are no longer in personal contact.
![Prince William, Prince Harry, Duchess of Sussex, the King](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000430339435_17877230872370_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq-PSyyIpYuv3hhTxnBm0pRlHmPOpeFd0SyQx9dn7kM_w.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Prince Harry is expected to embark on charity engagements including the WellChild awards in early September, while the Duchess is planning to continue her As Ever business.
The family is not yet known to have had formal changes to their security status, which has been decided on a case-by-case basis to date.
The Duke and Duchess married at St George’s Chapel, Windsor Castle, in May 2018.
In March 2019, Buckingham Palace announced they would set up their own household, breaking from the joint operation they had with the then Duke and Duchess of Cambridge.
In January 2020, the Duke and Duchess announced they intended to step back as “senior” members of the Royal family, become financially independent, still support Elizabeth II, but split their time between the UK and North America.
The late Queen ruled at the Sandringham summit, which was convened to resolve the crisis, that the couple could not be “half-in, half-out”.
By March 2020, they had set up a permanent home in California, officially stepped down as senior royals and stopped using their HRH styles.
Since their “farewell tour”, the Duchess has only returned to Britain with her husband for the late Queen’s funeral and a family holiday in July, when she did not join him in public.
summary: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have arrived in Britain at Birmingham Airport for an extended stay with their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet. The children are set to start at a British school the following week as part of an arrangement that will keep the family in the UK for an undetermined period. Despite allies suggesting the couple hopes for a part-time royal role, the King and Prince of Wales remain united in upholding the late Queen's Sandringham summit terms preventing a 'half-in, half-out' arrangement.
key_points: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex landed at Birmingham Airport on Wednesday for an extended stay in Britain.
Their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, will begin attending a British school at the start of the autumn term.
The couple plans to live internationally while maintaining their homes in California and Portugal, and will not resume working royal roles.
The King and Prince of Wales are united in upholding the Sandringham summit terms, meaning the Sussexes cannot adopt a part-time working royal model.

title: How Dolly Parton helped the world - from children's books to supporting Covid vaccine
author: Tiffany Wertheimer
content:
![Dolly Parton crouches down and speaks to several children. She has her arms around two of them.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/396c/live/3d980c40-a126-11f1-8c37-3f30331ac537.jpg)
The Imagination Library opened in the UK in 2007
- Published
Dolly Parton will not only be remembered for her iconic songs and Southern charm, but also for her philanthropic work.
Throughout her life, she supported communities in need, especially in her home state of Tennessee. She funded medical research that led to one of the first Covid-19 vaccines, donated to wildfire victims and even helped the once-endangered bald eagle, America's national bird.
But it is her Imagination Library - the mainstay of her charity work - that has helped millions of children learn to read by sending out free books.
The programme was inspired by her father who couldn't read or write.
"I think deep down inside, my daddy was prouder of [the library] than he even was of my career," she wrote.
Parton established her non-profit organisation, the Dollywood Foundation, in 1988, to help bolster children's education. Its efforts are practical - like sending out books - and often goes directly to the grass roots, where it can really make a difference, fast.
In the early 90s, Parton said she'd give every seventh and eighth-grade student (ages 12 to 14) in Sevier County, Tennessee, where she grew up, $500 if they graduated high school. They had to have a buddy, to keep each other in check - which in turn made more children graduate.
Sure, it was a bit of a bribe, but it worked - the drop out rate went from 35% to 6%, according to the foundation's website.
"I'm kind of addicted to the feeling of giving," she once said. "Knowing that I'm doing something good for someone else."
Parton was awarded the Carnegie Medal of Philanthropy in 2022, which honoured her as "one of the entertainment world's most generous philanthropists".
'All children should grow up in a home full of books'
Dolly Parton was one of 12 children born into a poor family that lived in a one-bedroom cabin in the Smoky Mountains. Her hardworking father, Robert Lee Parton, was a tobacco farmer.
"He was the smartest man I have ever known but I know in my heart his inability to read probably kept him from fulfilling all of his dreams," Dolly wrote.
Inspired by this, the Imagination Library was launched in 1995, with the help of Robert Parton. It sends out free books to children younger than five every month.
The programme was originally set up just for those in Sevier County - but it quickly went national and then global. The Imagination Library now sends books to children across the US, Canada, UK, Ireland and Australia.
According to its website, more than 332.4 million books have been sent out.
For many children who have never owned their own book, it is a special gift just for them.
"It's the fact they get recognised," Parton once said. "They get this little book with their little name on it in the mail, and they feel special... they know that somebody out there is thinking of them."
![Dolly Parton, wearing a black and white blazer, sits on a red leather chair and speaks to a crowd. There is a pile of old-style books next to her.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/0079/live/5374ea00-a12c-11f1-8c37-3f30331ac537.jpg)
In 2018, the Imagination Library donated its 100 millionth book to The Library of Congress in Washington DC
"That vision she had about books and this understanding of sharing stories was remarkable," Eileen Driver, the chair of the Stokesley Imagination Library in the UK, told the BBC's Radio Tees.
Scottish National Party councillor, Lee Mills - admittedly a superfan from a young age - said when he was elected he set out to bring the Imagination Library to Dundee.
"Dolly's legacy will last with every page turned of a children's book. I will do my utmost best to ensure that this is delivered to every child in Scotland," he told the BBC.
British author Selina Brown, whose book My Rice is Best was one of those selected to be distributed, told the BBC it was quite emotional to see 14,000 copies of her book being packed up, ready to post.
"For my book in particular, the protagonist is black. It helps with representation, it helps with real life situations and having a book that speaks directly to you and speaks to a different world is important."
During Covid, Parton started reading some of the books aloud, in recordings on YouTube for children - many of whom didn't know who she was.
"You mean she sings, too?" exclaimed one boy when he found out, Linda Jinnette Cooper wrote on the library's Facebook page.
Jolene turns to vaccine
Watch Dolly Parton sing a special vaccine edition of her hit song Jolene
In 2020, as the Covid-19 pandemic gripped the world, Parton encouraged people to get vaccinated and donated $1m (Â£716,000) to the Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville, which helped fund the Moderna vaccine.
A portion of the money went towards funding an early stage-trial of the Moderna vaccine, which found it to offer nearly 95% protection against severe Covid-19.
Reimagining her hit song, Jolene, Parton changed the lyrics to "vaccine, vaccine, vaccine, vaccine, I'm begging of you, please don't hesitate".
She showed herself being injected, saying: "I'm old enough to get it and I'm smart enough to get it."
Parton donated to medical research several times over the years.
A benefit concert in 2007 raised $1m for a new hospital and cancer centre in Sevier County, which includes a Dolly Parton Center for Women's Services.
Ten years later, she released a children's album, I Believe in You, and donated another $1m, this time to Nashville's Monroe Carell Jr. Children's Hospital at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, after her niece was treated for leukaemia there.
She donated yet another $1m to the hospital a few years later, this time to help paediatric infectious disease research.
"I love children," Parton said in a statement at the time. "No child should ever have to suffer, and I'm willing to do my part to try and keep as many of them as I can as healthy and safe as possible."
And earlier this year, the East Tennessee Children's Hospital announced it would be renamed to the Dolly Parton Children's Hospital, after the star partnered with the not-for-profit facility.
Supporting disaster victims
The Dollywood Foundation has a scholarships programme for high school seniors, which offers $15,000 to five students "who have a dream they wish to pursue".
It has also donated to the Salvation Army and helped the victims of several disasters in Tennessee.
After a deadly fire in Sevier County in 2016, Parton held a telethon that raised more than $13m. Kenny Rogers, Chris Stapleton, Reba McEntire and Cyndi Lauper were some of the big names who joined the event.
Parton continued her support by pledging $1,000 per month for six months to about 900 families who had lost their homes.
Five years later, when Middle Tennessee was devastated by flooding, Parton helped to raise $700,000 for residents.
"I'm just so proud to have been a part of anything that's good and that's making life a little better for people," she told Good Morning America the same year.
![A large statue of an eagle with spread wings is in the midst of a theme park swarming with visitors](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/5ceb/live/ad437290-a145-11f1-9311-09d4e1fc9016.jpg)
The bald eagle exhibit in Dollywood helps millions of people learn about America's national bird
Her Dollywood amusement park has a lot more than rollercoasters - it's also home to the largest sanctuary for non-releasable bald eagles in the world.
Managed by the American Eagle Foundation, its rehabilitation and breeding work has won awards and in 2007, the bald eagle was removed from the endangered species list.
In 2022, Parton's charity work to improve education was extended to adults, when it was announced that any Dollywood employee - whether they were seasonal, part-time or full-time, would have 100% of their tuition and books paid for if they furthered their education.
In announcing her death on Tuesday, Parton's team asked fans to donate to the Imagination Library, instead of sending flowers, so that her legacy can continue for many years to come.
"When I'm done, I can rest in peace knowing I've done my best," Parton once said.
"I hope that when my time comes, I'll leave something behind that others can use to lift themselves up."
Additional reporting by Olivia Ireland
- ![Dolly Parton with both arms raised on stage in 1983](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/a700/live/226708c0-a141-11f1-9311-09d4e1fc9016.jpg)
  - Published5 hours ago
 ![Dolly Parton smiling for the cameras while wearing a white sequined outfit at the Hollywood premiere of Joyful Noise in Los Angeles in 2012](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/bdeb/live/f73e1300-a11d-11f1-92eb-a9b3bbcf6f4a.jpg)
- ![Dolly Parton strums a guitar while looking to the right of frame wearing a blue top against a background of wooden panels on ABC TV in 1987.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/ede3/live/8fa98930-a10f-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
summary: Dolly Parton is celebrated not only for her music, but also for her extensive philanthropic work supporting education, medical research, and disaster victims. Her signature initiative, the Imagination Library, was inspired by her father and has sent hundreds of millions of free books to children globally. She also funded early-stage research for a Covid-19 vaccine, supported hospitals, and aided communities affected by wildfires and floods.
key_points: Dolly Parton's Imagination Library has distributed more than 332.4 million free books to children worldwide since its founding in 1995.
She donated $1m to the Vanderbilt University Medical Center, which helped fund early-stage trials for the Moderna Covid-19 vaccine.
Through the Dollywood Foundation, she established scholarship programs, supported disaster relief efforts, and funded multiple hospital and medical research centers.
Her Dollywood theme park houses the largest sanctuary for non-releasable bald eagles in the world, aiding in the recovery of the once-endangered species.

title: Heart, hope and a steely determination: Dolly Parton's musical legacy
author: Mark Savage
content:
![Dolly Parton with both arms raised on stage in 1983](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/a700/live/226708c0-a141-11f1-9311-09d4e1fc9016.jpg)
- Published
In 1980, Dolly Parton was filming her first Hollywood movie, 9 To 5, and between scenes she had an idea for the tune that would become the movie's theme song.
But her guitar was banned from the set - so she made the beat by strumming her acrylic nails together.
The sound, she realised, was just like the typewriter used by her character, a married secretary who is constantly belittled and sexually harassed by her boss.
Excited, she ran over and sang the song to her co-stars Lily Tomlin and Jane Fonda, who was also the film's producer.
"Lily and I looked at each other and we had goosebumps," Fonda said. "And we knew, this is not just a movie song, this is an anthem."
Released in November 1980, 9 To 5 became Parton's only US number one as a solo artist, and earned her an Oscar nomination for best song.
She loved to tell the fingernail story, but 9 To 5 has another legacy - for its powerful statements about working life and women's place in the corporate world.
You can probably sing the hook off the top of your head. "Working 9 To 5 / What a way to make a living!" It's jaunty and catchy. The sentiment is universal. Work sucks.
But dig deeper and Dolly's expressing real fury.
"It's a rich man's game, no matter what they call it / And you spend your life putting money in his wallet," she sings. "They just use your mind and they never give you credit."
The lyrics tapped into real frustrations and gave working women a voice.
But there's a reason why you might not have noticed the anger that fuels Dolly's song. She simply doesn't sing it that way - even though she had every right to, having navigated the sexism of the music industry from the age of 13.
Dolly Parton: The life of an iconic country singer
Her early breakthrough came in 1967 when she was hired as the "girl singer" on The Porter Wagoner Show, a TV showcase for country singer Porter Wagoner that reached millions of viewers each week.
Together, they released 21 hit duets including Just Someone I Used to Know, If Teardrops Were Pennies and Please Don't Stop Loving Me.
But as Parton's star rose, she began to outshine her co-star. Eventually, she realised she needed to strike out as a solo artist â writing I Will Always Love You as a letter of apology to her former mentor. He responded by suing her for breach of contract in 1979, demanding $3m (Â£2,2m).
Wanting to avoid a lengthy court battle, Parton settled for about $1m.
"I made up my mind that if he could live with it, I could live without it," she wrote in her autobiography. "I suppose Porter has done all right with it. I am neither his conscience nor his accountant."
It was typical of the star's ability to radiate cheery goodwill that she never held a grudge against Wagoner, always crediting him with giving her a crucial career break, even after their relationship fell apart.
Nobody's fool
But she was nobody's fool. Take, for example, the battle over the rights to I Will Always Love You.
After it hit number one in the country charts, Elvis Presley called â he loved the song and wanted to record a cover.
"You cannot imagine how excited I am about this," she told him. "This is the greatest thing that's ever happened to me as a songwriter."
But the night before the recording session, his notoriously hard-nosed manager, Colonel Tom Parker, called Parton and told her Elvis wouldn't record the song unless she handed over half of the lucrative publishing rights.
"I said, 'Well, that throws a new light on this. Because I can't give you half the publishing. I'm gonna leave that to my family,'" Parton told Reba McEntire's podcast in 2020.
"And he said, 'Well, then we can't do it.' And I cried all night."
"I mean, it was like the worst thing," she told Country Music Television. "People were saying, 'You're nuts. It's Elvis Presley. Hell, I'd give him all of it.'
"I said, 'I can't.' I always wondered what it would sound like. I know he would have killed it [in a good way]."
![Dolly Parton, pictured in black and white, rehearsing for her New York nightclub debut at the West Village's Bottom Line in 1977](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/885/cpsprodpb/9d81/live/0cd42c50-a13b-11f1-9d37-9b3d56456ba1.jpg)
But Parton had the last laugh.
When Whitney Houston recorded her blockbuster version of I Will Always Love You for The Bodyguard soundtrack in 1992, the country star still owned the rights and earned "enough money to buy Graceland", Presley's mansion.
Instead, she invested the money in a black neighbourhood in Nashville, Tennessee, saying she thought it was an apt way to honour Houston's legacy.
That determination to stand up for herself, and to value her music as more than just a commodity, is an essential part of Parton's legacy.
Without her example, would Taylor Swift have stood up to the hedge funds who bought her back catalogue, re-recording her biggest hits to rob them of royalties?
Perhaps not â but either way, Dolly approved.
"Smart!" she said when asked about Swift's masterplan. "She's so smart, she's so great, she's genius. I mean really, look at what she's doing! That's amazing!"
Mourning Parton's death, Swift acknowledged the star's "backbone of steel" in the struggle "to defend her own self worth as an artist".
![Dolly Parton gestures on stage at the 22nd annual Gay and Lesbian Alliance Against Defamation (GLAAD) Media Awards in Los Angeles, California in 2011](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/e404/live/6c3d9180-a13c-11f1-9311-09d4e1fc9016.jpg)
Musically, her legacy is just as profound.
Parton was about six years old when she wrote her first song: Little Tiny Tasseltop, an ode to her favourite doll and its corn-silk hair.
For the rest of her career, she turned everyday details like those into songs of hope and heart.
Her 1971 classic Coat of Many Colors tells the profoundly moving story of Parton as a child being proud of the ragged, hand-sewn clothes her mother had made for her.
The 1974 concept album My Tennessee Mountain Home, meanwhile, is a musical autobiography that opens with Parton reciting the first letter she wrote home after moving to Nashville as a teenager.
"A couple of folks already told me that they might record a couple of my songs, so I'll be makin' enough money to get by," she sang. "And I don't want you to be worrying about me bein' hungry or anything."
The album cover is a photo of the two-room log cabin that was Parton's actual childhood home in the 1940s and 50s, and the rest of the songs paint an idyllic picture of her childhood.
Even when the family didn't have electricity and running water, she was determined to see the good in everyone and every situation.
"We might have been poor but we didn't know it / We'd heard that word but we didn't know what it meant."
Inspired generations
Her diaristic approach to songwriting also gave birth to hits like Jolene â written about a red-headed love rival â and All I Can Do, a heartfelt declaration of love to her husband, Carl Dean.
Funny and authentic, she captured the trials and tribulations of life in a way that was always relatable, even when her stage outfits and her hairstyle remained larger than life.
The feminist message of 9 To 5 was preceded by When Possession Gets Too Strong and Just Because I'm A Woman, which castigated double standards in relationships: "My mistakes are no worse than yours / Just because I'm a woman."
And in an era where women were forced into gendered stereotypes â housewife, temptress, fallen woman, mixed-up girl â she satirised and sent up those roles, playing them to the hilt while emphasising her strength.
"I've always been misunderstood because of how I look," she sang on 2008's Backwood Barbie. "Don't judge me by the cover, cos I'm a real good book."
Words like those inspired generations of women to be who they were, not who the world perceived them as.
And she used her music to unite people, even as much of the country music establishment entrenched itself in conservatism.
In 2002, at the House of Blues in Los Angeles, Parton even replaced the name Jolene with "drag queen" as a crowd of drag performers looked on.
Outside music, her philanthropy gave scholarships to impoverished students and supplied more than 200 million books to young readers.
Significantly, none of the country stars she inspired were ever billed as "the next Dolly Parton" because no-one did it like Dolly. She was unique. Irreplaceable. Unreproducible.
A legend in her lifetime, and now beyond.
summary: Dolly Parton built a legendary musical and cultural legacy defined by her sharp business acumen, fierce independence, and deeply personal songwriting. From creating the iconic feminist anthem "9 To 5" to protecting her publishing rights against industry pressures, she consistently stood up for her self-worth as an artist. Through her authentic storytelling, philanthropy, and ability to navigate industry sexism with grace, Parton has deeply inspired generations of women.
key_points: Dolly Parton wrote her hit song "9 To 5" while filming her first movie, mimicking the sound of a typewriter by strumming her acrylic nails together.

She famously turned down Elvis Presley's offer to cover "I Will Always Love You" because his manager demanded half of her publishing rights, a decision that later paid off when Whitney Houston recorded the track.
Parton's diaristic songwriting style turned everyday childhood memories and personal experiences into relatable hits like "Coat of Many Colors" and "Jolene."
She has maintained ownership of her work and fiercely defended her artistic value, inspiring future generations of musicians like Taylor Swift.
Beyond her music career, Parton has a rich history of philanthropy, including supplying millions of books to young readers and funding scholarships.

title: Backwoods Barbie and the ‘God almighty’ PMS Blues: Dolly Parton’s 10 best deep cuts
author: Jenny Stevens
content:
Down from Dover (1970)
Dolly Parton was one of the most gifted narrative lyricists ever – particularly when it came to telling the stories of women’s experiences. This is one of her more harrowing stories about a young woman (see also: The Bridge). Some will recognise this as a track on Nancy Sinatra and Lee Hazlewood’s album Nancy and Lee (where the backing singing is replaced with sweeping orchestra). But the clarity of Parton’s voice on the original, taken from her fifth album, 1970’s The Fairest of Them All, is staggering.
The lyrics follow a young woman who gets pregnant out of wedlock – by a man who has promised to return home before she starts to show. We listen as ominous clouds cast shadows over the fields the young woman can see from her window: the seasons change, and her man does not return. She is sent away to have the child in secret, to hide her parents’ shame, but her daughter is stillborn. Parton’s voice cracks as she delivers one of the final lines about the devastation unfolding for her protagonist, as she turns to her baby: “I guess she knew she’d never have her father’s arms to hold her.”
PMS Blues (1994)
Recorded for her 1994 live album Heartsongs: Live From Home, you can hear the audience at Dollywood roar and cackle through this stomping blues number (just wait until she gets to the line about menopause). “I got those God almighty, slap somebody, PMS Blues,” she growls. There’s gags about fluid retention, mood swings, headaches and telling kids to hide from their hormonal mothers. “It’s the only time in my life I ever think about wishing I’d been a man,” she rails. It’s wild, rollicking fun.
The Bargain Store (1975)
While some would say this isn’t a deep cut, given it’s the title track of her 15th album, I’d argue it’s still an unsung gem. Melodically, it’s got the lightness of touch of Love Is Like A Butterfly, released a year earlier, but it’s lyrical heft is something else entirely. This is a story of an older woman, someone whose heart had been dragged around the block, whose dreams have been smashed and whose plans for a better life ground into dust.
The metaphor is not subtle – a woman with a history is a bargain store and all her merchandise is used and cheap – but it’s a wry take on how society treats a fallen woman, and the madonna/whore complex by which, perversely, both virginity and sex sells. The protagonist invites people to view her merchandise which, with a little care and mending, could be as good as new. “I can guarantee you’ll be completely satisfied,” she sings.
Is it bizarre? Absolutely. But it also speaks to the craven nature of women as commodities, as well as the more complex sense of longing for our broken woman to find someone who might help fix her. It’s a different tone to Parton’s more famous takedowns of rampant double standards, such as the perfect Just Because I’m A Woman, which is a direct conversation with the men who walk off and leave a woman they’ve got into trouble.
Daddy Come and Get Me (1970)
It begins with a perfect slide guitar and a startling opening line setting the scene: “In this mental institution…”
This track, also from 1970’s The Fairest of Them All, is firmly in the country music tradition of mining the deepest despair for a very visceral kind of art.
Our protagonist has been put in a psychiatric hospital by her partner but, as she says, it’s not her mind that’s broken, it’s her heart. She pleads for her father to come and get her. She needs help, she says, “but not this kind”. She is powerless, looking to another male figure in her life to love and care for her.
The spoken word part of this song sees Parton deliver a heartbreaking, poetic and raw performance, much like in her opus I Will Always Love You.
Wildflowers (1987)
I’ve turned to this song at periods of rupture and upheaval in my life. Written by Parton, it features on the 1987 album Trio, a holy trinity of a collaboration between country music titans Parton, Emmylou Harris and Linda Ronstadt. Parton sings in the first person here, a younger version of herself, wild-eyed and full of promise, who takes to the road to escape the confines of her family. Like the seeds of a wildflower, she catches the wind and takes to the road. And we know it’s going to be OK because, as she says, “wildflowers don’t care where they grow”. It’s a song that agitates for change, and gives the listener the courage to go forth.
The Pain of Loving You (1971)
If there ever was a song that captures the fracturing of a relationship, with all its complexities and power plays and love-hate ferocity, this is surely it. This song featured on the album Two of a Kind, the sixth of an eventual 13 albums Parton would release with her one-time mentor, Porter Wagoner. He was one of the biggest country stars of the 60s and 70s who brought her in to perform on his weekly hit TV show in her early career. However, as Parton’s fame began eclipse Wagoner’s, he sought to control her, and their relationship strained to the point of snapping in 1974, when she left the show. Parton’s vocal harmony skips over Wagoner’s with the levity of a bird skimming water, as she sings the blow: “To love and hate at the same time / the line between the two is fine”.
Light of a Clear Blue Morning (1977)
I heard Parton’s soaring gospel song used in a 2021 revival of Larry Kramer’s autobiographical play The Normal Heart, about the Aids epidemic in early 1980s New York, at London’s National Theatre. As the lifeless body of a bright and brilliant young man who was taken so cruelly lays on a bed on the stage, a rendition of this song plays. It is one of the most moving moments of theatre I have ever seen. While a hit on the country charts in the US, it never had mainstream chart success. Featuring on Parton’s 1977 album New Harvest… First Gathering, she often said it was about her rebirth after the fraying of her relationship with Wagoner. When she says she can finally see the light of a clear blue morning, it’s impossible not to believe her. It is pure, exhilarating hope pressed into vinyl.
Backwoods Barbie (2008)
Another theme in the Parton catalogue is her ability to pre-empt any sexist, presumptive comments by making herself the butt of the joke first – and the joke would be funnier than anyone else could dare make. She did it from the off with her early hit Dumb Blonde – and boy did it show she was, as she sang, “nobody’s fool”. Backwoods Barbie, the titular track from her 2008 album, was a riotous return to country after a decade of bluegrass and folk records. “Don’t let these false eyelashes lead you to believe / That I’m as shallow as I look ‘cause I run true and deep,” she sings.
The Bridge (1968)
Featuring on 1968’s Just Because I’m a Woman, Parton’s second album, this eerie song is another story about a young woman in trouble. Parton’s protagonist and her beau meet on a bridge at night, the moon is bright, and “desire swept through us”. A nearby meadow is sought, and you can guess the rest. The final verse sees the woman alone, pregnant, her feet creeping further to the edge of the bridge. And then the song ends as abruptly as The Sopranos and as mystically as Bobbie Gentry’s Ode to Billy Joe, another mysterious song about events on a bridge. “Here is where I end it,” Parton sings. Then snap, silence. We will never know what happened.
Here I Am (1971)
Originally an album track on her 1971 album Coat of Many Colors, this song was revived for the soundtrack of the 2018 film Dumplin’ when Parton and Sia recorded a cover. The original, in my opinion, is Parton’s answer to Let It Be or Hey Jude in terms of anthem status. It’s more than a song, it’s a call to action and a cry for communion. “Here I am, reaching out, to give you love that you’re without,” she sings in its glorious, rousing chorus. Because what was Dolly Parton if not a hand reaching out in the dark – one of wisdom, calm, unity. Here I am, she sings. And that is where she will always be, in that voice, in those songs.
summary: This article explores ten deep cuts and lesser-known tracks from Dolly Parton's extensive musical catalog. It highlights her storytelling prowess, emotional depth, and ability to address complex themes ranging from heartbreak and societal double standards to mental health and personal rebirth.
key_points: Down from Dover (1970) and The Bridge (1968) feature harrowing narratives about young women facing tragic circumstances.
PMS Blues (1994) is a comedic, blues-inspired live track addressing fluid retention, mood swings, and menopause.
The Bargain Store (1975) uses the metaphor of a used merchandise store to critique societal views on fallen women.
Daddy Come and Get Me (1970) and Wildflowers (1987) touch upon themes of despair in a psychiatric hospital and the liberating urge to escape confinement, respectively.
Light of a Clear Blue Morning (1977) and Backwoods Barbie (2008) highlight Parton's themes of personal rebirth and preempting sexism with humor.

title: 11 huge EastEnders spoilers for next week (August 31 to September 3)
author: Sophie Dainty
content:
EastEnders spoilers follow.
Next week on EastEnders, Nicola's chaotic family arrive in Walford, armed with a big secret.
Meanwhile, Ravi makes a shocking discovery, and Linda struggles with her feelings for Max.
Here is our round-up of all the biggest moments coming up in Albert Square. You can also check out our collection of 27 spoiler pictures for next week's episodes.
1. The Hawkins family arrive in Walford
Nicola's sisters Gemma and Jodie return to Albert Square.
Gemma's son Ryder is also with them and the clan make their presence known immediately.
Nicola agrees to let them stay on one condition – their estranged mother Rose doesn't turn up as well.
Despite the promise, Ned – Gemma's husband – soon turns up with Rose, leaving Nicola furious.
2. Nicola is urged to build bridges
Nicola refuses to let her family stay with her, forcing Gemma and Ned to consider other options.
Harry steps in to offer Ryder and Jodie a place to stay but urges Nicola to sort things out with Rose once and for all.
3. Ned spots a familiar face
Ned apologises to Kat about the disruption his family caused when they arrived on the Square.
However, he gets a surprise when he spots Alfie – a face from the past.
Nicola is unsettled when she later finds her family gathered in The Vic. She then gets a further shock when she learns that Alfie has offered Gemma and Ned a place to stay.
4. Priya struggles to keep her secret
Ravi urges Priya to tell the kids about their engagement.
When Priya later spots Chelsea and Vicki planning Kim and Howie's wedding, she asks to join them. It's not long before Cindy is asking for help with hers as well.
Feeling nauseous, Priya steps outside, where she bumps into Penny, who questions what's going on with her. Priya ends up telling Penny that she is pregnant but swears her to secrecy.
5. Rose continues to cause problems
Rose is continuing to cause chaos at Peacock Palace, leaving Linda and Elaine desperate to get rid of her.
Wanting to ease the tension, Gemma reaches out to Nicola but it's not long before she's clashing with Rose as well.
The Hawkins family later hatch a risky plan to resolve things between Nicola and Rose, but it just makes everything worse.
6. Priya makes a big decision
Priya catches Nugget dealing weed and scolds him, prompting Max to step in.
Later, Priya recognises how much progress Ravi has made and decides to tell the kids about their engagement.
7. Ravi makes a shocking discovery
Ravi is delighted that his engagement to Priya is now out in the open but still wants to know about the man she was seeing.
When Max walks Priya home that evening, they share a moment outside her home, which is witnessed by Ravi.
Afterwards, Ravi grows increasingly suspicious of Max and continues to watch him closely.
8. The Hawkins' secret is revealed
Kat makes it clear that Gemma and Ned can't stay at The Vic for a second night.
The couple are relieved when Nicola has a change of heart and agrees to let them stay on a temporary basis.
However, Nicola soon learns the real reason why the Hawkins have arrived in Walford.
9. Max and Linda grow closer
Clive steps in and saves the day when a power cut threatens Linda and Elaine's bingo event.
Linda agrees to another date with Clive, but later shares a moment with Max when he helps Ollie on his first day of secondary school.
10. Max and Howie prepare for their stag
Kim is disappointed by the focus on Max's stag and pushes Howie to socialise more.
Taking matters into her own hands, Kim tasks Denzel with planning his dad's night.
Feeling out of his depth, Denzel approaches Oscar about combining the stags, which he agrees to.
But what does Oscar have in store for Max?
11. Linda struggles with her feelings
As Linda prepares for her date with Clive, she is left torn over her true feelings when she learns how Max played a key role in saving the community centre.
When Clive soon arrives with confirmation that the centre is now secure, Linda feels more conflicted than ever.
But with Max preparing for his stag, has she missed her chance with him?

title: The wit and wisdom of Dolly Parton: 'If you want the rainbow, you gotta put up with the rain'
author: Helen Bushby; Paul Glynn
content:
![Dolly Parton smiling for the cameras while wearing a white sequined outfit at the Hollywood premiere of Joyful Noise in Los Angeles in 2012](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/bdeb/live/f73e1300-a11d-11f1-92eb-a9b3bbcf6f4a.jpg)
- Published
Dolly Parton, the much-loved US singer-songwriter who has died at the age of 80, was known for her pearls of wisdom and humour as well as her music.
She regularly offered her perceptive and witty insights about life, music, fame and equal rights.
Here are some of her most memorable quotes from down the years:
Philosophy
- "The way I see it, if you want the rainbow, you gotta put up with the rain."
- "I always just thought if you see somebody without a smile, give 'em yours!"
- "I'm not going to limit myself just because people won't accept the fact that I can do something else."
- "If you don't like the road you're walking, start paving another one."
- "Don't get so busy making a living that you forget to make a life."
- "Storms make trees take deeper roots."
- "Sometimes, what would look like to be my biggest mistakes turn out to be my biggest blessings."
On songwriting and performing
- "I actually take my songwriting more serious than anything else I do, so I would say I am a songwriter first."
- "It's my way of expressing myself. It's my therapy."
- "You have to search for a long time because I've written a lot of songs. But yes, there are pieces of me, of course, in everything I write."
- "I have to write and sing. See, that was my first love, and I have to do that forever, however I have to do it."
- "I look totally artificial, but I am totally real, as a writer, as a professional, as a human being. A rhinestone shines just as good as a diamond."
- "My dream was always to make as many people happy as I could in this life."
- "I always count my blessings, more than I count my money. I don't work for money, never did. It was the art, it was the job. I loved the work. And I've done well, and I'm thankful for it."
- "I wanted more than to just be a farmer's daughter, even though I'm proud to be [one]. I just wanted pretty things. I wanted money to buy the things I had always been impressed with as a child. I wanted, I guess, to be a star."
On her image
- "If I was trying to describe myself to someone that had never seen me before, I would say, 'Calm down. Don't get scared. It's just me. I know I look totally bizarre and artificial, but I'm totally real inside.'"
- "I'm not offended by all the dumb blonde jokes because I know I'm not dumb - and I'm not blonde either."
- "It costs a lot of money to look this cheap."
- "People always ask me how long it takes to do my hair. I don't know, I'm never there."
- "If I see something sagging, bagging and dragging, I'm going to nip it, tuck it, and suck it."
- "I don't like to be like everybody else. I've often made the statement that I would never stoop so low as to be fashionable. That's the easiest thing in the world to do."
- "I make jokes about it, but it's the truth that I kind of patterned my look after the town tramp. I didn't know what she was, just this woman who was blond and piled her hair up, wore high heels and tight skirts, and, boy, she was the prettiest thing I'd ever seen. Momma used to say, 'Aw, she's just trash', and I thought, 'That's what I want to be when I grow up. Trash.'"
- "I'm pretty sharp. I'm not educated and I'm not that intelligent, but I'm smart. They say somebody's street smart. I feel like if I got intelligence, it's just a country smart."
- Journalist: "What is the trait you most deplore in yourself?" Dolly: "The fact that sometimes my mouth is a little too big and a little too open and sounds too much like a sailor."
- "I'm very real where it counts, and that's inside."
![Dolly Parton wearing a black jacket while attending a party following the opening night of 9 to 5: The Musical in Los Angeles in 2008](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/8236/live/5212ca50-a11e-11f1-92eb-a9b3bbcf6f4a.jpg)
On love, life and death
- "They say love isn't about two people gazing into each other's eyes, it is about two people gazing outwards in the same direction. I believe this with all my heart."
- "I never really tried to hide myself from anybody. I think that's one of the reasons I'm still around, people feel like they know me."
- "I don't want to be a star if I have no life."
- Speaking more about the book gifting programme for children: "Since I had no kids and my husband was pretty independent, I had freedom. So I think a big part of my success is the fact that I was free to work. And I didn't have children, because I believe that God didn't mean for me to have kids, so everybody's kids could be mine, so I could do things like the Imagination Library."
- "I ain't never gonna be old because I ain't got time to be old. I can't stop long enough to grow old. I'm just gonna be the best I can be at whatever age I am."
- "When I'm done, I can rest in peace knowing I've done my best. I hope that when my time comes, I'll leave something behind that others can use to lift themselves up."
- "When I die, I'll really be getting to live then because I believe that there is a greater place than this".
- Journalist: "What would be her funeral song?" Dolly: "I don't know - but I won't be singing it!"
On LGBT and black rights
- "Yes, I support gay marriage. They have every right to be as miserable as straight people."
- "And of course black lives matter. Do we think our little white asses are the only ones that matter? No!"
- "I've got transgender people. I've got gays. I've got lesbians. I've got drunks. I've got drug addicts - all within my own family. I know and love them all, and I do not judge."
- "It's a good thing I was born a girl, otherwise I'd be a drag queen."
Advice to younger fans
- In a letter to young recipients of books from Dolly Parton's Imagination Library: "You and all of your friends are very special. There is no limit to what you can do or how far you can go."
- She continued: "Just remember the lessons my family taught me - dream big dreams; learn everything you can learn; and care for all those who care for you. You do all of these things and you can be anyone you want to be.
- "You are terrific, and remember... I will always love you."
summary: Dolly Parton, the celebrated US singer-songwriter who passed away at the age of 80, was widely known for her humor, wisdom, and candid observations on life, music, and fame. Throughout her career, she shared perceptive insights regarding her art, her distinctive artificial image, and her personal philosophy. She was also known for voicing her support for equal rights, including LGBT and Black lives.
key_points: Dolly Parton passed away at the age of 80.
She considered songwriting to be her primary focus and a form of therapy.
She famously described her outward appearance as artificial while maintaining that she was entirely real on the inside.
She openly expressed support for gay marriage, Black lives, and members of the LGBT community.

title: Dolly Parton tributes: Elton John, Oprah Winfrey, Taylor Swift, Sabrina Carpenter and Paul McCartney
author: Sareen Habeshian
content:
Dolly Parton: The life of an iconic country singer
- Published
Sir Paul McCartney, Oprah Winfrey, Taylor Swift, BeyoncÃ© and Sir Elton John have led a wave of tributes to music icon Dolly Parton, honouring her impact across the globe.
The Beatles legend called Parton a "magnificent star", Oprah said she "brought the light" and the Rocket Man singer dubbed her a "giant of an artist" who was "irreplaceable".
Parton died on Tuesday at the age of 80, after "a brief battle with cancer", her team said in a statement to CBS, the BBC's US partner.
Tributes have poured in from US presidents across the political spectrum and musicians across all genres, remembering her not just for her award-winning career, but her philanthropy and humble nature that transcended country music.
![Elton John and Dolly Parton perform "Turn the Lights Out When You Leave" and "Imagine" (Photo by Michael Loccisano/FilmMagic for Country Music Association)](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/944/cpsprodpb/6457/live/eb67dad0-a0db-11f1-bf7e-3dee971383e9.jpg)
Sir Elton John and Parton preformed together in 2005 at the annual Country Music Association Awards
McCartney reflected on his history with Parton, which began when he met her in Nashville at the Grande Ole Opry right before starting her solo musical career.
"She was so bubbly and full of life, it is difficult to take in the news that she has passed," he said. "Her songwriting, her singing and her philanthropy were unrivaled in the world of country music and it is hard to imagine living in a world without Dolly."
John said he was "shocked and devastated" over the news. "A giant of an artist - unique and irreplaceable, with the kindest heart".
Swift, who began her professional career in country music as a teen after moving to Nashville, has paid tribute to Parton's "true grace and true grit, all in one dazzling person".
"A world without Dolly doesn't feel possible, real, or right," the singer said in a statement shared with the BBC. "But because of the eternally generous way she spent her time on this earth and the countless lives she changed for the better, her legacy will be an everlasting one."
As well as "melodies and lyrics she wrote that thawed even the coldest of hearts," Swift acknowledged "the millions of books she provided children all over the world so that they might fall in love with stories the way she did".
She thanked Parton "for the tightropes she walked so that young girls like me could grow up dreaming of joining the circus too".
BeyoncÃ© said Parton was the "barometer" and the "north star".
"Bold and brilliant. Talented and tenacious. You taught so many lessons on how to be uniquely oneself. I am grateful for your art, your heart, your generosity, your humor, your entrepreneurship," BeyoncÃ© wrote.
Cowboy Carter, BeyoncÃ©'s 2024 country album, famously featured a rendition of Parton's song Jolene.
Former talk-show host Winfrey wrote that one of her fondest memories with Parton was "having a hoot and a holler while wearing Bob Mackie gowns on her show Dolly".
"This girl from the Smoky Mountains of Tennessee dreamed a life and then lived a life bigger than she could have ever imagined, giving so generously to others in ways we saw and ways we didn't."
![Dolly Parton and Miley Cyrus performed at the 61st Annual Grammy Awards in 2019.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/f52f/live/16fe19b0-a0f1-11f1-8872-c736a901bba9.jpg)
Dolly Parton and Miley Cyrus performed at the 61st Annual Grammy Awards in 2019
Parton's musical influence spanned generations, even inspiring the careers of a younger wave of female talent, including pop stars Sabrina Carpenter and Miley Cyrus.
The pair collaborated in 2025 for a country-inspired remix and music video of Carpenter's hit song Please Please Please.
"The only thing I could say after we first met was 'she really is an angel walking the earth' and 'we look like we could be sisters!'" Carpenter wrote on Instagram.
Along with behind the scenes pictures of the pair filming their music video, Carpenter added: "Your light will be something the world will search forever to find again."
Singer Miley Cyrus is Parton's goddaughter. The pair teamed up on a new version of Cyrus's 2013 song Wrecking Ball â and Parton appeared on several episodes of Hannah Montana, in which Cyrus starred.
Cyrus's father and Parton's close friend Billy Ray Cyrus remembered the music icon as being "part of our lives, on our TV's, right in our living rooms".
"I have so many moments and memories with Dolly, it's hard to know where to start," Billy Ray Cyrus said. "Like every little boy, I grew up loving Dolly Parton."
He recounted a time when he had to apologise to Parton for tabloid rumours which claimed he was having an affair with her.
"In true Dolly fashion, she just looked at me, winked and said: "Honey, this trash sells records!"
![Reba and Dolly are pictures holding up two golden awards on a red carpet.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/d5b9/live/a5780650-a0d9-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
McEntire collaborated with Parton multiple times over their careers and shared being honoured by the Academy Of Country Music Awards in 2017.
The wave of musical talents honouring Parton has stretched from fellow country star Reba McEntire to rapper Eminem, with each sharing personal stories on how important the late singer was to them and the world as a whole.
McEntire thanked Parton for "all the wonderful things you did for us here on earth. "Your love, your music and you gave so much with your huge huge heart. There will never ever be another you".
"We will remember and cherish every memory and every note you ever played and sang," McEntire wrote. "Thank you, Lord, for Dolly. She's gonna have a blast in heaven singing all her favorite songs with all her family and friends who have gone on before her."
Rapper Eminem noted that even while he had never met Parton, she still made her mark on his life with a note she sent calling him "very special".
"I'm sorry we never got a chance to meet, but getting this note from Dolly really had a an impact on me. She definitely didn't have to take the time to do it," he said, posting a photo of a letter from her congratulating him on his induction in the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame.
"Even for a kid who mostly listened to rap music, she was an icon," he added. "A superstar in every sense. Rest easy Dolly. And thank you for the kind words."
![After her performance at the Bottom Line, American Country musician Dolly Parton is seen hugging British rocker Mick Jagger backstage, New York, New York, May 14, 1977](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/683/cpsprodpb/aa56/live/e5505d80-a0da-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Parton embraced Jagger backstage in New York after a show in 1977.
Rock star Melissa Etheridge said "words fail me today", adding she felt "blessed with knowing her, just a little. We all were. I will strive the rest of my days to be as joyful and loving as she was".
Sir Rod Stewart said he was "absolutely floored" and Rolling Stones legend Mick Jagger called her a "wonderful songwriter and singer" who "brought so many people together". Cyndi Lauper said it was "hard for me to imagine the world without Dolly," noting she was a "role model for all of us" who made her constantly stop to think: "What would Dolly do?"
Cuban-American singer Gloria Estefan said her "heart was heavy", noting Parton's legacy was "so much more" than her musical career.
"She was a force of nature whose enormous talent was matched by an even bigger heart," Estefan wrote. "She brought joy, laughter, comfort and inspiration to generations, always with that unmistakable warmth, wit and authenticity that made everyone feel like they knew her."
The massive number of tributes showed how beloved Parton was across all genres, countries, and political beliefs - and among celebrities and fans across multiple generations.
From Australia's prime minister Antony Albanese to elected officials from both sides of US politics shared their affection for the icon, both her music and her lifetime of supporting causes such as children's literacy and women's health.
US President Donald Trump called her death a "true loss for millions of people. There has never been anyone like her, and never will". He ordered American flags across the US to be lowered in her memory - a rare honour that is mostly reserved for elected leaders and other officials in the US government.
"Rest in Peace, Dolly! The World loves you," the Republican US president added in a social media post.
Former US President Bill Clinton, a Democrat, called Parton "one of a kind â a great songwriter and performer who told the stories of everyday Americans with honesty, humility, and heart". He noted that while her star grew, she "never forgot where she came from" and always gave back through her philanthropic efforts.
Clinton said he and his wife, former US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, were big fans and first saw Parton perform in 1974.
The world of country music, meanwhile, mourned one of its biggest icons, with singer Kacey Musgraves, who performed in a 2019 Grammys celebration of the singer she frequently covers, saying: "The world feels a lot less sparkly all of a sudden."
Keith Urban, who collaborated with Parton, was "heartbroken" by the news, and said that "honestly... I have no words right now".
![Dolly Parton and Keith Urban performing on stage](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/98ec/live/70d43ba0-a0c3-11f1-b8cc-1bd2cc322bf4.jpg)
Country singer Blake Shelton, who worked with Parton on the American television series The Voice wrote: "I can say with absolute certainty that we are all feeling the same heart brokenness today."
"I want everyone to know that she was the EXACT person that you think she is," he added. "It was like being with the funnest, most loving, most caring and closest member of your family."
On social media, American singer and actress Dionne Warwick said her "heart is heavy".
"I will certainly miss her laughter, jokes and her being. Rest well and in total peace my friend," she wrote.
Former wife of Elvis Presley, Priscilla Presley, recalled: "After Elvis and I left the courthouse following our divorce, he sang [I Will Always Love You] to me as we walked down the steps together."
"Her music touched all of us, but it was Dolly's warmth, humour and enormous heart that made her truly one of a kind," Presley added.
Parton, who was known for her roles in the movies 9 to 5 and Steel Magnolias, as well as the show Hannah Montana, was remembered fondly by many actors.
Seth MacFarlane said that when working with Parton, who guest-starred on his show The Orville, "her kindness, generosity, and authenticity were evident from moment one".
"I'm devastated. Truly", actress Keke Palmer said alongside a photo of her and Parton. The pair starred in the 2012 musical Joyful Noise.
Actress Jamie Lee Curtis said Parton was a hero who "is a great example for us all".
Fashion designer Donatella Versace said: "The world has lost one of the kindest and most generous of souls, the greatest of story tellers and a true legend of music."
summary: Legendary country music icon Dolly Parton has died at the age of 80 following a brief battle with cancer. A massive wave of global tributes has poured in from musicians, actors, and political figures across the political spectrum. Admirers remembered her not only for her award-winning music and songwriting career, but also for her humility, entrepreneurship, and extensive philanthropy.
key_points: Dolly Parton passed away at age 80 following a brief battle with cancer.
Music legends including Sir Paul McCartney, Sir Elton John, Taylor Swift, and Beyoncé paid tribute to her lasting global impact.
Politicians from various backgrounds, including US President Donald Trump and former President Bill Clinton, honored her legacy and charitable work.
Collaborators and peers highlighted her kindness, philanthropy, children's literacy efforts, and unique ability to transcend musical genres.

title: North West says she’s ready for a ‘regular job’ next year after canceling tour
author: Carsen Holaday
content:
North West, 13, reveals she wants to work at Starbucks next year: ‘I want to have a regular job’
![North West, 13, reveals she wants to work at Starbucks next year: ‘I want to have a regular job’](<https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/07/31/10/12/north-west-kardashian-9e2ec03b.jpeg?quality=75&width=83&auto=webp 83w>)
North West says she’s ready for a ‘regular job’ next year after canceling tour
- North West, the 13-year-old daughter of Kim Kardashian and Kanye West, revealed she wants to work as a Starbucks barista next year to experience having a regular job.
- Speaking to Dazed magazine, West clarified that music remains her primary passion and life goal after releasing her debut album N0rth4evr in May.
- “I still wanna work,” the teen told the outlet. “I wanna work at, like, Starbucks next year. I think I can next year ‘cause I’m gonna be 14, so… I think I can.” “I want to have a regular job, I guess,” she added.
- The young artist has already made notable stage appearances at major music festivals, including Rolling Loud and Lyrical Lemonade's Summer Smash.
- The interview follows the abrupt cancellation of her first headlining 14-date North American tour alongside Molly Santana earlier this month. Beyond music, West is expanding her creative pursuits into fashion after her family filed trademark applications for a brand named NOR11.
summary: Thirteen-year-old North West revealed in a Dazed magazine interview that she wants to work at Starbucks next year to experience having a regular job. The announcement follows her recent debut album release and the cancellation of her first headlining North American tour. Despite her desire for conventional employment, she emphasized that music remains her primary passion.
key_points: North West expressed a desire to work as a Starbucks barista next year when she turns 14.
The 13-year-old is the daughter of Kim Kardashian and Kanye West.
She recently released her debut album titled N0rth4evr in May.
The interview follows the cancellation of her first headlining 14-date tour.
